topics.description: Metadata API â€” export const metadata / generateMetadata â€” plus Open Graph/Twitter cards, JSON-LD structured data, sitemap.ts, robots.ts, and canonical URLs.
keyConcepts: Why CSR-only content is a problem for crawlers
commonMistakes: relying on <title> in a client component; forgetting canonical URLs with query-param variants; dangerouslySetInnerHTML with interpolated user text in JSON-LD (XSS); indexing ?page=2 duplicates; assuming crawlers render.
practiceTasks: build /products/[slug] with generateMetadata (title template, canonical, OG image, robots: noindex for discontinued items), JSON-LD Product with offers, sitemap.ts generated from the DB, and robots.ts disallowing /admin. Then curl the HTML and confirm every tag is in the *initial* response, not added by JS. Finally, run a Google rich-results-style validator or a structured-data linter and fix what it flags.

interviewQuestions.text: How do you set page metadata dynamically?
What are Open Graph and Twitter cards for?
How do you generate a sitemap without hand-writing it?
Why does CSR-only content hurt SEO?
interviewQuestions.answer: *Context.* A marketing page renders its content only after a client-side fetch; traffic is fine but organic traffic is flat and link previews are blank. *Decision.* Server-render or prerender anything indexable, and treat client fetching as an enhancement. *Reasoning.* Crawlers vary in whether and how well they execute JavaScript; social scrapers generally do not execute it at all; and even JS-capable crawlers allocate limited rendering budget and penalize failures or errors during hydration. Content that depends on hydration is therefore discovered later, indexed less reliably, and never seen at all by non-executing scrapers. The specific failure here â€” blank link previews â€” is a direct consequence: the OG tags that would produce the preview are either absent from the initial HTML or the preview scraper sees an empty body. *Trade-offs.* Server-rendering the content costs TTFB and server compute versus a static shell; prerendering (SSG/ISR) gets most of the SEO benefit at near-zero cost but requires build-time or revalidation-time data access, which means a build can fail on stale or unavailable data and dynamic segments need generateStaticParams. *Failure scenario.* A redesign converts every page to CSR with useEffect fetching; rankings drop 30% over two months, and the diagnosis is confusing because "it works in the browser" and Core Web Vitals in the field are fine. *Prevention.* Put indexable content in the server/prerendered path, assert in CI that key pages contain the expected text in the raw HTML response, keep generateMetadata server-side, and monitor crawler logs for 5xx/JS errors.

Self-hosting gotchas
output: 'standalone' bundles a minimal server (node server.js) with only the traced dependencies â€” smaller images. Set HOSTNAME, PORT, and copy public/ and .next/static alongside.
Static assets must be served by your CDN/reverse proxy, not the Node process: /_next/static/* are content-hashed and immutable; cache them for a year. Serve HTML with no-cache so the CDN revalidates.
The image optimizer needs a shared cache across replicas (see 4.2.9) and enough memory (sharp/libvips). If you don't want to run it, disable it and use a CDN image service.

Don't cache per-user HTML. Any route reading cookies must send Cache-Control: private, no-store and be excluded from CDN caching.

Then verify a deploy: (1) assets are cached, (2) HTML revalidates, (3) a Suspense page streams (watch curl -N), (4) a per-user page is never CDN-cached, (5) memory stays flat under image load. interviewQuestions.text: Vercel vs self-hosted: what decides it?

Managed platforms give you global CDN, integrated ISR, the image optimizer, edge middleware, and PR previews with near-zero ops, at the price of per-invocation pricing above free tiers and framework lock-in. Self-hosting gives you full control, predictable cost at scale, and the ability to sit inside existing compliance and networking constraints, but you now own the CDN cache headers, the image optimizer's memory and shared cache, the ISR cache store, and streaming buffering. topics.referenceMarkdown:
**Definition:** Deployment is the set of decisions about where the Next.js server runs, how it is built and started, and how caching/CDN layers sit in front of it.

### Vercel vs self-hosted

| Concern | Vercel (or a similar managed platform) | Self-hosted Node / Docker |
|---|---|---|
| Setup | Zero config, preview deploys per PR | You own Dockerfile, build, process manager, autoscaling |
| ISR / on-demand revalidation | Built in; `revalidateTag` invalidates the global cache instantly | You must run a cache store you control and wire invalidation to it |
| Image optimization | Built-in service, global | Local `/_next/image` service; needs memory/CPU and a shared cache |
| Middleware / Edge | Managed edge network | You self-host or use a CDN edge function |
| Caching | Managed CDN with `x-nextjs-cache` observability | Your CDN (Cloudflare, Fastly, CloudFront) plus correct `Cache-Control` |
| Cost | Simple at low volume, can surprise at high volume | Cheaper at scale, but you pay ops |
| Lock-in | High | Low |
| Control | Limited (config file, no custom server runtime) | Total |
| Best for | Fast iteration, marketing sites, small teams, preview-per-PR | Cost at scale, compliance, custom networking, existing k8s |

**Static export.** `output: 'export'` in `next.config.ts` produces a pure static site in `out/`: no Node server, so no SSR, no ISR, no middleware, no Server Actions, no route handlers, no image optimization (or images must be pre-optimized yourself). Use it for docs sites and blogs where everything can be built. Everything dynamic must move to a client fetch or a separate backend.

**Self-hosting gotchas**
1. **`output: 'standalone'`** bundles a minimal server (`node server.js`) with only the traced dependencies â€” smaller images. Set `HOSTNAME`, `PORT`, and copy `public/` and `.next/static` alongside.
2. **Static assets must be served by your CDN/reverse proxy**, not the Node process: `/_next/static/*` are content-hashed and immutable; cache them for a year. Serve HTML with `no-cache` so the CDN revalidates.
3. **The image optimizer needs a shared cache** across replicas (see 4.2.9) and enough memory (`sharp`/libvips). If you don't want to run it, disable it and use a CDN image service.
4. **ISR/on-demand revalidation needs a persistent cache store** shared across instances, otherwise invalidation is per-instance and your behaviour is nondeterministic under load.
5. **Don't cache per-user HTML.** Any route reading cookies must send `Cache-Control: private, no-store` and be excluded from CDN caching.
6. **Streaming requires disabling response buffering** in nginx (`proxy_buffering off;`) or your Suspense benefits vanish.
7. **Timeouts and long actions:** platforms kill long requests; enqueue instead.
8. **Env vars:** build-time (`NEXT_PUBLIC_*`) are inlined into the bundle and are public; runtime secrets must be read server-side only.

### Preview deployments
A good CI setup builds the app, runs lint/typecheck/unit/e2e, deploys a preview with a real database branch or fixture data, runs Playwright against it, then merges. The interview-relevant point: preview environments are how you catch "works locally, breaks in production" caching and env problems before users do.

**Questions**
1. Vercel vs self-hosted: what decides it?
2. What does `output: 'standalone'` do?
3. What breaks with `output: 'export'`?
4. How should you set cache headers for `/_next/static` vs HTML?
5. Why does self-hosting ISR get flaky?
6. What nginx setting matters for streaming?
7. How do you prevent a CDN from caching per-user pages?
8. What are preview deployments for?
9. How do you handle secrets with `NEXT_PUBLIC_`?
10. What is the image-optimizer memory story?

**Model answer, Q1:** "It is a cost/complexity/lock-in tradeoff. Managed platforms give you global CDN, integrated ISR, the image optimizer, edge middleware, and PR previews with near-zero ops, at the price of per-invocation pricing above free tiers and framework lock-in. Self-hosting gives you full control, predictable cost at scale, and the ability to sit inside existing compliance and networking constraints, but you now own the CDN cache headers, the image optimizer's memory and shared cache, the ISR cache store, and streaming buffering. My default for a new product is managed; my default for a large existing platform with k8s and traffic is self-hosted."

**Mistakes:** caching HTML at the CDN without `private` markers; buffering streaming responses; running the image optimizer on every replica with no shared cache; expecting on-demand revalidation to be global on a multi-replica self-hosted setup; putting secrets in `NEXT_PUBLIC_*`; forgetting `public/` and `.next/static` in the Docker image.

**Mini task:** containerize with `output: 'standalone'`, put nginx in front, and configure: immutable 1-year caching for `/_next/static`, `no-cache` for HTML, `proxy_buffering off`, and a `/health` route on the Node process. Then verify a deploy: (1) assets are cached, (2) HTML revalidates, (3) a Suspense page streams (watch `curl -N`), (4) a per-user page is never CDN-cached, (5) memory stays flat under image load. Write the cache header table you settled on.

topics.title: Meta-Frameworks, React 19 Interplay, and Partial Prerendering
topics.description: Meta-Frameworks, React 19 Interplay, and Partial Prerendering within Next.js and Meta-Frameworks.
keyConcepts: What "meta-framework" means
The honest comparison
React 19 interplay
useActionState replaces useState + manual pending for form actions: you get a state object that includes pending, the returned state, and the error.
useFormStatus gives pending inside a child of the form (also data, method, action), so you can build a submit button that knows it is submitting.

Form action prop: <form action={fn}> where fn can be a Server Action or a client function. Server Actions *are* React 19 form actions, which is why progressive enhancement works: without JS the browser posts to the action endpoint.

useOptimistic for optimistic UI driven by an action's pending state â€” the framework gives you a temporary optimistic value that reverts if the action fails, which is a better default than hand-rolled rollback.
use() reads a promise (including one created during render) and suspends â€” the basis for reading data without async in the component, useful in client components.
Streaming and transitions are more capable in React 19: <Suspense> boundaries can be revealed out of order, and transitions are more interruptible, which is what makes Next's navigation feel instant.
Partial Prerendering (PPR) â€” awareness
commonMistakes: declaring one framework universally best; ignoring that migrations cost behavior, not just syntax; over-claiming PPR as stable; treating useOptimistic as a substitute for a server-authoritative re-read.
practiceTasks: build the same CRUD "notes" app twice: once in Next.js App Router with Server Actions and ISR, once in React Router 7 framework mode with a loader and an action. Diff them on: lines of data-fetch code, where caching lives, how a mutation invalidates a read, and how hard it is to reason about staleness. Then write one paragraph justifying your choice for a specific product, citing evidence from the exercise.

interviewQuestions.text: What is a meta-framework?
How does React Router 7 framework mode differ from Next's data model?
When is Astro the right choice?
What does React 19 add for forms and actions?
What is `useActionState` and how does it differ from `useFormStatus`?
What does `useOptimistic` do, and is it safer than manual rollback?
What is `use()` for?
What is Partial Prerendering and what problem does it solve?
Why is "which framework is best" a bad interview answer?
What would make you leave Next.js for another meta-framework?
interviewQuestions.answer: *Context.* I'm the frontend lead on a large React/TypeScript product with heavy e-commerce traffic, a small team, and an existing Next.js codebase. *Decision.* I would not migrate on preference; I would migrate only if a specific, measurable blocker appears. *Reasoning.* The migration cost is not the framework â€” it is re-deriving caching semantics, auditing every data access, retraining the team, and re-tuning SEO and Core Web Vitals with a real regression budget. That cost is justified only when a capability we need is unavailable or a specific defect is unfixable: for example, if we need a data model we can fully understand and audit (React Router's loader/action split makes every request's data flow explicit and greppable, whereas Next's caching is rule-based and has changed defaults across versions), or if the App Router's implicit caching has repeatedly produced production staleness incidents we cannot prevent. *Trade-offs.* On the other side: React Router gives up the managed edge/CDN/image/ISR integration and the hiring pool; keeping Next means living with its abstractions and version churn. *Failure scenario.* A rewrite "because the framework is wrong" ships three months late, misses the holiday traffic window, and the new app has worse LCP because nobody carried over image and streaming work. *Alternative.* Incremental mitigation inside Next: add explicit caching documentation, tag discipline, and staleness alerts; adopt new features route by route; evaluate a *carve-out* (a docs or marketing site in Astro, a widget in React Router) rather than a whole-app rewrite. *Signals I would actually act on:* repeated data-leak or staleness incidents, a framework limitation blocking a roadmap item with real revenue behind it, or hiring/velocity data showing the framework is the constraint.

interviewQuestions.text: How does the App Router's implicit caching compare with React Router's explicit loaders?

**What "meta-framework" means.** A framework that owns routing, rendering strategy, data fetching, and build-time optimization, driven by conventions. The category's real split: | Framework | Model | Rendering strengths | Choose it when | |---|---|---|---| | **Next.js** | React, RSC, server-first | Hybrid rendering (static/ISR/SSR/CSR) in one app; huge ecosystem; strong SEO defaults | You want maximum flexibility and are on React/TypeScript | | **React Router 7 (framework mode)** | React, loaders/actions, based on Remix | Simple mental model: `loader` per route, nested, forms as first-class; less framework magic | You want the App Router's ergonomics without the caching-opacity; you know Remix; you like explicit data flow | | **Remix** | Predecessor of RR7 framework mode | Same loader/action model; mature; the original "web-first" framework | Existing Remix apps; you value the explicit loader/action split | | **Astro** | Islands architecture; multi-framework | Ships zero JS by default; islands; content-focused; great Markdown/MDX | Content sites, marketing, docs, blogs; you want minimal JS and don't need a big app | | **Nuxt** | Vue | Analogous hybrid rendering, SSR/SSG/SPA modes | You are on Vue | | **SvelteKit** | Svelte | Compiles away; very small runtime; excellent DX | You are on Svelte, or you want the smallest client runtime | | **SolidStart** | Solid | Fine-grained reactivity, no virtual DOM | You want fine-grained perf and like Solid | **The honest comparison.** No one of these is "better". They differ in where they place the abstraction boundary: React Router 7 makes data flow explicit (`loader` returns data, `action` handles mutations â€” you can read the whole request lifecycle), Next.js makes data flow implicit (data is fetched wherever it is rendered, cached by rules you must learn). Next wins on ecosystem, image/edge/CDN integration, and hiring pool; React Router wins on explicitness and a smaller conceptual surface; Astro wins on shipping zero JS; SvelteKit wins on client runtime size. A senior answer names the tradeoff, not a winner. **React 19 interplay.** React 19 formalizes what Next's Server Actions were built on: - **`useActionState`** replaces `useState` + manual pending for form actions: you get a state object that includes `pending`, the returned state, and the error. - **`useFormStatus`** gives `pending` inside a child of the form (also `data`, `method`, `action`), so you can build a submit button that knows it is submitting. - **Form `action` prop**: `
` where `fn` can be a Server Action or a client function. Server Actions *are* React 19 form actions, which is why progressive enhancement works: without JS the browser posts to the action endpoint. - **`useOptimistic`** for optimistic UI driven by an action's pending state â€” the framework gives you a temporary optimistic value that reverts if the action fails, which is a better default than hand-rolled rollback. - **`use()`** reads a promise (including one created during render) and suspends â€” the basis for reading data without `async` in the component, useful in client components. - **Streaming and transitions** are more capable in React 19: `` boundaries can be revealed out of order, and transitions are more interruptible, which is what makes Next's navigation feel instant. ```tsx 'use client'; import { useActionState, useOptimistic } from 'react'; type Msg = { text: string; pending?: boolean; error?: string }; export function Chat({ roomId, send }: { roomId: string; send: (fd: FormData) => Promise }) { const [messages, formAction, isPending] = useActionState(send, []); const [optimistic, addOptimistic] = useOptimistic( messages, (state, newMsg: Msg) => [...state, { ...newMsg, pending: true }], ); return (
    {optimistic.map((m, i) => (
  • {m.text}{m.error ? ` â€” ${m.error}` : ''}
    • ))}
); } ``` **Partial Prerendering (PPR) â€” awareness.** The idea: split a route's render into a *static shell* (prerendered at build time, cacheable globally) and *dynamic holes* (streamed per request inside ``). A product page's shell â€” layout, nav, product title, image â€” is prerendered and served from the edge; the personalized "your cart" widget and live price are holes streamed per request. Result: static-cacheable latency with per-request freshness. It requires explicit opt-in via cache directives/`` boundaries (in newer Next versions, Cache Components / `dynamicIO` and `'use cache'`), and it is still evolving â€” verify the current status in the Next.js docs (Cache Components, PPR preview/blog) rather than asserting specifics. The interview-worthy insight: PPR makes the caching boundary a *developer-marked region* rather than a per-route setting, which is the same philosophical shift as RSC: explicit boundaries beat implicit global defaults. **Questions** 1. What is a meta-framework? 2. How does React Router 7 framework mode differ from Next's data model? 3. When is Astro the right choice? 4. What does React 19 add for forms and actions? 5. What is `useActionState` and how does it differ from `useFormStatus`? 6. What does `useOptimistic` do, and is it safer than manual rollback? 7. What is `use()` for? 8. What is Partial Prerendering and what problem does it solve? 9. Why is "which framework is best" a bad interview answer? 10. What would make you leave Next.js for another meta-framework? 11. How does the App Router's implicit caching compare with React Router's explicit loaders? **Model answer, Q10 (senior/staff framing):** *Context.* I'm the frontend lead on a large React/TypeScript product with heavy e-commerce traffic, a small team, and an existing Next.js codebase. *Decision.* I would not migrate on preference; I would migrate only if a specific, measurable blocker appears. *Reasoning.* The migration cost is not the framework â€” it is re-deriving caching semantics, auditing every data access, retraining the team, and re-tuning SEO and Core Web Vitals with a real regression budget. That cost is justified only when a capability we need is unavailable or a specific defect is unfixable: for example, if we need a data model we can fully understand and audit (React Router's `loader`/`action` split makes every request's data flow explicit and greppable, whereas Next's caching is rule-based and has changed defaults across versions), or if the App Router's implicit caching has repeatedly produced production staleness incidents we cannot prevent. *Trade-offs.* On the other side: React Router gives up the managed edge/CDN/image/ISR integration and the hiring pool; keeping Next means living with its abstractions and version churn. *Failure scenario.* A rewrite "because the framework is wrong" ships three months late, misses the holiday traffic window, and the new app has worse LCP because nobody carried over image and streaming work. *Alternative.* Incremental mitigation inside Next: add explicit caching documentation, tag discipline, and staleness alerts; adopt new features route by route; evaluate a *carve-out* (a docs or marketing site in Astro, a widget in React Router) rather than a whole-app rewrite. *Signals I would actually act on:* repeated data-leak or staleness incidents, a framework limitation blocking a roadmap item with real revenue behind it, or hiring/velocity data showing the framework is the constraint. **Mistakes:** declaring one framework universally best; ignoring that migrations cost behavior, not just syntax; over-claiming PPR as stable; treating `useOptimistic` as a substitute for a server-authoritative re-read. **Mini task:** build the same CRUD "notes" app twice: once in Next.js App Router with Server Actions and ISR, once in React Router 7 framework mode with a `loader` and an `action`. Diff them on: lines of data-fetch code, where caching lives, how a mutation invalidates a read, and how hard it is to reason about staleness. Then write one paragraph justifying your choice for a specific product, citing evidence from the exercise. --- ---

groups.title: State Management
groups.description:
State Management within React Deep Dive.

---

ðŸŸ¡ Intermediate Â· **Must-know** Â· Prerequisites: 4.1.14 (Context), 4.1.10 (memoisation)

**What state management actually is.** Not "a place to put data". It is the set of decisions that answer four questions for each piece of data in the application:

1. **Where does it live?** Component, lifted parent, context, a global store, the URL, or the server.
2. **Who may write it?** One component, or many (and does order matter)?
3. **How does it change?** Immutably replaced, mutated in place, pushed by an event, or pulled by a render.
4. **What invalidates it?** A refetch, a full reload, a sign-out, a TTL, or never.

A library is just a default answer to (1) and (4). Choosing well means choosing the *right default*, or choosing no default at all.

**The three-layer model used throughout this section**

```
Layer 3  Remote truth        the database                owned by the server
Layer 2  Cache of remote     TanStack Query / RTK Query   invalidated, TTL'd, deduped
Layer 1  Client state        route params, form input,    owned by the browser,
                             UI flags, wizard step        dies with the tab (or not)
Layer 0  Derived             totals, filtered lists,      recomputed, never stored,
                             canSubmit, breadcrumbs       never a source of truth
```

Errors are almost always a violation of this model: storing layer 3 in layer 1, storing layer 0 in layer 1, or letting two layers write the same fact.

---

topics.title: The state taxonomy: local UI state, derived state, server state, URL state, global client state
topics.description: State taxonomy is the practice of *classifying every piece of state in the app* into exactly one of five kinds, each with a different owner, lifetime, persistence rule, and tool. Getting the classification right removes most state-management debate, because each kind has a defensible home and the home is not negotiable by preference.
keyConcepts: The mechanics of why the classification matters
Local UI state fails when you *lift it too far*. The classic symptom is prop drilling six levels to set a boolean. Fix: composition, a custom hook with its own state, or colocate the state.

Derived state fails when you *store* it in useState and keep it in sync with an effect. This creates a second source of truth that is wrong for exactly as long as the effect takes to run â€” and wrong forever if the dependency is missed. Fix: delete the state and compute it.
Server state fails when you store it in useState. Then you own caching, deduplication, staleness, garbage collection, retries, and cross-component sharing, badly. Fix: use a query cache.
URL state fails when you keep it in a store. Then the back button breaks, the page cannot be shared, refresh loses it, and SEO/analytics cannot see it. Fix: put it in the URL.
Global client state fails when it becomes a dumping ground for layer 2 and 3. Fix: enforce the boundary â€” a store must not hold server data.

Local UI state: default for anything one subtree cares about. Do not use for: anything two distant components need (that is lifted, or a store, or the URL), anything derivable, or anything another engineer will need to find (put it in a feature folder, not scattered useStates).
Derived state: always prefer computing. The only reason to useMemo is cost; the only reason to keep it in state is that it is *not* actually derived (it was user input).
Server state: always via a query library or a framework loader. "Always" except in throwaway demos and tests.
URL state: anything shareable, bookmarkable, or that should survive refresh; also anything that changes what the *server* renders (SEO). Not: secrets, and not transient hover/animation flags.
Global client state: last resort after lifting and Context fail. Justify it with a concrete requirement ("five routes deep, changes at 60 Hz, and never persisted").
Production and operational
commonMistakes: Storing a *filtered list* in state next to the unfiltered list ("keep the same reference when unchanged" is a symptom of a duplication bug).
Storing isLoading / error next to the data instead of using the query's own status object â€” you now have three places that can disagree.
Keeping page/filter state in a store "just for the session", so it survives navigation into a route that should have been fresh.
Using useState + useEffect to mirror a prop into state instead of using a key or the prop.
Classifying a WebSocket buffer as local UI state.
naming five kinds and then putting all five in one store; calling derived state "state"; using a store as a cache without a staleness policy; URL state that includes anything the user should not see.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain the mechanics of why the classification matters and when you would use it.
Explain production and operational and when you would use it.
Explain "what is derived state and what goes wrong when you store it?" and when you would use it.
Explain "how do you decide something is server state?" and when you would use it.
Explain "your filter resets when the user clicks a row and comes back â€” whose bug is that?" and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: A taxonomy with five buckets costs a little classification discipline up front and buys: no stale-copy bugs, back-button correctness for free, shareable URLs for free, cache hits for free, and a codebase where a reader can *guess* where any value lives. The cost is that you sometimes route trivial values through the URL (verbose URLs) or keep tiny state in a store (global mutable surface). Both are acceptable; debugging two sources of truth for one fact is not.

topics.title: Context: the right use, the wrong use, and the performance cliff
topics.description: Context is a *push-based* dependency-injection and read-through-broadcast channel: a provider publishes one value; every descendant that calls useContext for that context is notified when the published value changes identity. It solves "get a value to a distant descendant without prop drilling". It is not a state manager, and using it as one is the single most common React performance incident.
keyConcepts: Subscription is by context, not by prop. When a Provider's value prop changes (Object.is fails against the previous render's value), React walks its subtree and marks *every fiber that reads that context* for re-render. React.memo is irrelevant: memo compares props, and a context broadcast is not a props change.

Propagation is a tree walk, not a subscription registry. With many providers/consumers this is why React can start tearing across concurrent rendering â€” hence useSyncExternalStore (see below) as the safe way to expose an *external* mutable store.

value identity is the change signal. value={{ user }} creates a new object every render, so *every* consumer re-renders on *every* provider render, regardless of whether user changed. This is the performance cliff.
The escape hatch: context over an external store
Production and operational
"Explain exactly why memo does not protect a context consumer."
"Your theme provider wraps the whole app; the app feels sluggish on the settings page. Diagnose."
"When would you *not* reach for Context even though you could?"
"How does useSyncExternalStore change Context's behaviour, and what does getServerSnapshot do?"
"What is the difference between a stable context value and a memoised one?"
commonMistakes: value={{ ... }} without useMemo â€” the cliff, in its purest form.
One context holding both items and dispatch, so dispatch-only consumers re-render on every item change.
Context for server data: no dedupe, so ten components using the same context fire ten requests, or one request whose result nobody can refresh.
Setting state on the context *value object* (ctx.items.push(...)) â€” mutating a shared reference that Object.is considers unchanged.
Reading a context in a component you do not control just to get a theme, when CSS custom properties would do it with no re-render at all.

assuming Context is scoped to a "component boundary" (it is not â€” it is subtree-wide); forgetting that reading a context makes the component a consumer even if the read is conditional; using Context as a cache.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain production and operational and when you would use it.
Explain "explain exactly why memo does not protect a context consumer." and when you would use it.
Explain "when would you *not* reach for context even though you could?" and when you would use it.
Explain "what is the difference between a stable context value and a memoised one?" and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: Context is ~zero-dependency, type-safe, built in, and the right answer for roughly 30% of "shared state" needs. Its costs: broadcast invalidation (a cliff, not a slope), no devtools, no middleware, no time travel, no persistence, and no way to subscribe to a *slice*. The upside of a store is the mirror image: precise subscriptions and tooling, paid for with a dependency and a ceremony that small apps do not need.

topics.title: Redux Toolkit: store shape, slices, createSlice, createAsyncThunk, RTK Query
topics.description: Redux Toolkit (RTK) is an opinionated layer over Redux that (a) removes the boilerplate that made Redux unpopular, (b) makes the store a *single immutable state tree* changed only through serialisable actions, and (c) ships two libraries on top: createAsyncThunk for imperative async workflows and RTK Query for declarative server-state fetching with caching, deduplication, invalidation, and normalised caching. RTK 2.x targets Redux 5 and React 18+.
keyConcepts: Store shape â€” the contract you are signing
Typed hooks â€” non-negotiable
createSlice â€” one file per feature
createAsyncThunk â€” the thunk middleware in a typed wrapper
RTK Query â€” the modern answer for "Redux + server state"
queryKey = (endpointName, serialisedArgs). Two hooks with equal args = one request, one cache entry. Different but overlapping args = two cache entries (the classic "list and detail drift" bug).
providesTags describes what the entry depends on; invalidatesTags invalidates. This is a *dependency graph*, coarse-to-fine, and it is the whole invalidation story.

Cached data is returned for a subscription and re-fetched when stale (keepUnusedDataFor governs eviction of *unsubscribed* entries; refetchOnMount/refetchOnFocus/refetchOnReconnect govern revalidation of used ones).
transformResponse is for shaping one shape into another. Never use it to merge two caches; use providesTags.
onQueryStarted is the optimistic-update hook. It gets { dispatch, queryFulfilled, getState } and its returned promise resolves when the query settles.

.selectFromResult narrows what a component subscribes to, which is the single most effective RTK Query performance lever (selectFromResult: ({ data, isLoading }) => ({ users: data?.users, isLoading })).
Production and operational
commonMistakes: Hand-rolled fetch in a thunk *and* RTK Query in the same app â€” two caches, two staleness policies.
Passing a class instance or Date in an action payload and disabling the serialisable check instead of fixing it.
Mutating outside a reducer (a reducer that mutates the action payload, or store.getState().x = 1 anywhere).
useSelector(s => s.users.items) where items is an array rebuilt on every state change â€” the component re-renders forever (see 4.3.4).
returning a fresh object from a selector: useSelector will loop under useSyncExternalStore.
Using combineReducers with a top-level array of "panes" instead of keyed slices â€” the array becomes the bottleneck and the reducer non-deterministic.
Assuming store.getState() is fresh inside a reducer (it is not â€” use the state argument).

using Redux for everything "because it scales"; writing fetch logic by hand when RTK Query exists; believing createSlice makes mutation impossible (Immer handles it, but only *inside* reducers); storing secrets in the store.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain store shape â€” the contract you are signing and when you would use it.
Explain typed hooks â€” non-negotiable and when you would use it.
Explain createslice â€” one file per feature and when you would use it.
Explain createasyncthunk â€” the thunk middleware in a typed wrapper and when you would use it.
Explain rtk query â€” the modern answer for "redux + server state" and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: Redux's costs are real: ceremony (file per slice), an indirection between a click and a render, dispatch typing overhead, and a bundle cost you do not pay with Zustand. Its benefits are also real: one mutation path, one DevTools timeline, deterministic replay, serialisability as an architectural constraint, and RTK Query's cache and invalidation graph. Net verdict that a senior engineer would give: *Redux pays for itself in codebases with many writers of shared state and a real DevTools dependency; it is overkill for a five-screen app with two forms.*

topics.title: Selectors, reselect, memoisation, and normalized state
topics.description: A *selector* is a pure function from state to a value. *Reselect* is a memoisation library that makes selectors cheap by caching on their inputs. *Normalized state* is the shape where entities live in a keyed map (byId: Record<Id, T>) plus an array of ids, instead of being duplicated inside every parent object.
keyConcepts: The problem selectors solve
Why "cache size 1" is usually right
Parameterised selectors in components â€” the React version
Normalized state â€” the shape that makes everything else possible
Which one
When to normalise and when not to
Production and operational

RTK Query already returns normalised results internally (result.ids / result.entities) â€” do not duplicate that work by normalising again. If you need a different shape, use transformResponse and keep the adapter as the only writer.
Enforce the shape in review or lint: a createEntityAdapter slice plus a no-restricted-syntax rule banning .find( on entity arrays.

Log selector recomputation counts in dev (a console.count in a development-only branch) to find accidental createSelector calls inside components â€” creating a selector per render defeats all memoisation.
For very large normalised collections, Object.freeze in dev (RTK does this in development) so accidental mutation fails loudly.
"Why does useSelector re-render constantly here, and what are the two possible fixes?"
commonMistakes: Calling createSelector *inside* a component (new cache every render).
A selector that takes state and returns state.a.b.filter(...) â€” a new array per call.
Mixing shapes: usersById plus a users array that can disagree.
Deep-cloning in a selector to "fix" mutation (structuredClone in a selector destroys identity and perf).

Using useSelector(shallowEqual) from React Redux as a universal fix instead of memoising â€” it is correct but costs a full shallow comparison per store update for every subscriber; a memoised selector is cheaper and narrower.
Using normalizr where you only need one level (a plain Map and two reducers are enough).
treating reselect as a correctness mechanism rather than a performance one; normalising lists where order is the data; writing selectors in components; returning object literals from useSelector.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain the problem selectors solve and when you would use it.
Explain why "cache size 1" is usually right and when you would use it.
Explain parameterised selectors in components â€” the react version and when you would use it.
Explain normalized state â€” the shape that makes everything else possible and when you would use it.
Explain which one and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: Normalisation costs indirection: every read is byId[id], every write is one function, and a component that wants a tree needs a denormalize/join step (which must itself be memoised). The payoff is that a single write updates every view, entity updates can be subscribed to per-id (useAppSelector(s => s.users.entities[id]) â€” one user's change does not re-render a list of a thousand), and list operations stop being O(nÂ²) find/includes calls. Selectors trade a memory cost and a dependency list for "recompute only when inputs changed"; the failure mode is a wrong dependency, which returns stale data â€” so keep input selectors trivially correct (one property access each) rather than clever.

topics.title: Middleware: thunk vs saga vs listener middleware, and when you need any
topics.description: Redux middleware is a function that wraps dispatch and can do work before, after, or instead of passing the action along:
keyConcepts: The three flavours
Listener middleware â€” the modern default for "when X happens, do Y"
Sagas â€” when the flow genuinely is a sequence of events
Which one to pick
Production and operational

topics.title: Zustand, Jotai, MobX, Recoil: comparison and selection criteria
topics.description: Four "minimal global state" libraries that all try to beat Redux's ceremony while keeping a global store. They differ in the *unit of state*: a store with selectors (Zustand), an atom graph (Jotai), observable objects with a reaction system (MobX), and atom graphs with dependency tracking + selectors (Recoil).
keyConcepts: Mechanical comparison

Team familiarity and hiring. The single biggest factor. A bespoke Zustand store is 40 lines of convention; a MobX codebase needs someone who can reason about observability. Optimise for the five people who will maintain it.

Do you need to *derive* state reactively and often? Jotai's derived atoms or MobX computed earn their keep if you have chained derivations. If derivations are one-liners in useMemo, plain Zustand is fine.

Do you need fine-grained reactivity on large collections? MobX tracks per-property reads inside a render and re-runs only what depends on what changed â€” the best model for a virtualised list or a spreadsheet-like grid. Zustand's selector is per-component, which is nearly as good with a good selector.

Do you need middleware, devtools time travel, and a big team on a large app? Redux Toolkit. It is the only one of the four with a first-party DevTools timeline, serialisability enforcement, and a documented answer to "who dispatched this".
Do you need cross-cutting async workflows (4.3.5)? Redux Toolkit, or RTK Query. Zustand can do it (store.getState().doThing()) but there is no equivalent of predicate/effect/cancelActiveListeners.
Do you need the smallest possible bundle? Zustand (~1.5 kB gz) â‰² Jotai (~3 kB) â‰ª MobX (~15 kB) â‰ª Recoil (~25 kB).

Bundle + SSR? Jotai and Recoil need Provider with an initial-state prop; Zustand's vanilla store makes SSR hydration explicit; MobX needs enableStaticRendering(typeof window === 'undefined') on the server.

"What is Recoil's status today?"
"How does MobX know what to re-render?"
"Why does useStore with an object selector loop?"

Persisting functions or Date objects with zustand/persist (JSON round-trip destroys them silently).
Using useAtom (read+write) where useAtomValue/useSetAtom would do, subscribing to reads you never use.
MobX without runInAction after an await, or with enforceActions: 'observed' and mutation inside a render.
Using MobX/Jotai to cache server data.
Writing to the same key from two stores in an app that has "one store per team" as a rule â€” the merge problem.
citing bundle sizes you have not verified; proposing Recoil for a new build; using any of them as a cache; evaluating on "Redux vs Zustand" tribalism instead of requirements.

tradeoffs: Zustand: least ceremony, most examples, best default; costs: no built-in devtools time travel, patterns emerge by convention. Jotai: the cleanest derived-state story and the best TypeScript inference; costs: a second mental model (atoms vs stores) and a smaller ecosystem. MobX: the most powerful and least-buggy reactive model once you understand it; costs: bundle size, decorator-era baggage in docs, and a class-based store that some teams dislike. Redux Toolkit: the most explicit and most inspectable; costs: files and ceremony. Recoil: superseded.

topics.title: XState and state machines: when a finite state machine beats booleans
topics.description: A finite state machine (FSM) models a system as a *finite set of states* plus a *finite set of transitions* between them, where transitions may be guarded and may perform effects. XState is the reference implementation for React/TS. It replaces "a pile of booleans that can contradict each other" with "one state value that cannot".
keyConcepts: The bug an FSM eliminates
state.matches({ playing: {} }) tests the state value. state.matches('playing') for a top-level string. There is no way to be "half in a state".
Events are the only input. The machine is a pure function of (state, event). Side effects happen only in actions and invoke.
assign is the only way to change context, and it must be written as a function of (context, event) so it stays serialisable and pure. assign({ x: 5 }) is sugar for a constant assignment.
Guards are predicates evaluated *before* a transition is taken; the first matching entry in an array of transitions wins, so order matters.
States can be nested ({ idle: { on: { FOCUS: 'editing' } }, editing: { initial: 'clean', states: { clean: {...}, dirty: {...} } } }), giving compound states without multiplying values.
invoke ties a service's lifetime to a state: when the machine leaves loading, the fetch is aborted (onError with an abort must be filtered, or use the signal).
after is a delayed transition, cancelled if the state is left first â€” the built-in answer to "clear this timeout in cleanup".
always transitions are evaluated on every event while in a state (guards that fire immediately); history states let you resume where you were; choice picks one of N transitions.
When a machine beats booleans, precisely
Production and operational
"When is a state machine better than booleans? Give a case where it is worse."
commonMistakes: Modelling a machine with on: { EVENT: ... } transitions that don't have targets (side-effect-only transitions), which makes the state chart a lie.
Using guard to mutate instead of guard + assign.
Forgetting that invoke's promise keeps running after you leave the state unless you pass the signal through.
Deep nesting states so that state.matches('editing') is true for six visually different screens.
Building an FSM for a resource that has no interesting transitions.
Writing machines inside components (recreated every render); define them at module scope.
over-applying FSMs; treating a machine as async-by-default; assuming matches() handles nested states without care; not persisting long flows.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain the bug an fsm eliminates and when you would use it.

Explain "how does an fsm help with 'ignore the double click'?" and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: You gain: impossible states rendered impossible, explicit and testable logic, guaranteed cleanup via state-scoped invoke/after, a single place to see every legal transition, and trivially inspectable debugging (state.value is a data value). You pay: a steeper learning curve, a second mental model (event/action/service), serialisation if you want to resume a machine mid-flow (persisted State), heavier code for simple cases, and a smaller talent pool. The judgement call is about *transition complexity*, not state count.

topics.title: URL as state, localStorage persistence, and hydration-safe storage
topics.description: Two persistence mechanisms with opposite visibility. URL state is state the user can see, copy, bookmark, share, and go back from â€” it lives in location, survives everything, and requires zero storage. Client storage (localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB, a cookie) is state the user cannot see, which survives a refresh, is scoped to an origin, and is *not* part of the document.
keyConcepts: URL as state â€” the mechanics and the rules
Anything a user might want to send someone goes in the search params. Not in a store, not in localStorage.

push vs replace is a product decision, per interaction. Typing in a search box, changing a filter, paginating: replace, so the back button leaves the *page* rather than walking through 40 filter states. Following a result, opening an item, submitting a form: push.

Params must be canonical. /invoices?page=1 and /invoices should be the same screen; parse to defaults on read, serialise by omitting defaults on write. Non-canonical URLs split analytics funnels and create duplicate-content SEO issues.
Server-renderable. Query params must decide *what the server returns* (pagination, filters), otherwise SEO and share-links show page 1 while the URL says page 3.
Never put a secret in a URL â€” query strings appear in Referer, browser history, and server logs (cross-ref 4.6.9).
Parse, don't spread. Validate params into a typed object at the route boundary with a schema (Zod, 4.4.8) so ?page=abc cannot become NaN.
localStorage â€” the API and its limits
Versioned persistence with migration
Cookies as the third option
What belongs where â€” a table you can defend
Production and operational
commonMistakes: Writing to localStorage during render (side effect in render; StrictMode double-writes).
Reading localStorage during render on the server path â†’ ReferenceError or hydration mismatch.
Persisting the entire store (including server cache) with no version and no migration.
pushing every keystroke of a search box into history (back button becomes unusable).
Storing tokens in localStorage (any XSS exfiltrates them for the life of the token).
Expecting cross-tab listeners to fire in the writing tab (they do not).
Copying URL params straight into a query key without validation (NaN, Infinity, __proto__).
treating the URL bar as decoration; persisting unvalidated blobs; assuming storage is per-tab; using push for every filter tweak.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain url as state â€” the mechanics and the rules and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: URL state costs verbosity (?tab=history&sort=-created), requires you to parse/validate/serialise, and can produce unfriendly URLs that you must design (path vs query, short keys vs readable keys). It buys shareability, back-button correctness, SSR/SEO, analytics attribution, and survival across devices â€” five things localStorage cannot buy. localStorage costs synchronous main-thread reads, cross-tab coupling, an untrusted-by-your-own-app JSON blob, XSS exposure, and versioning burden. It buys survival across reloads for *invisible preferences*.

topics.title: Optimistic updates and rollback
topics.description: An optimistic update applies the expected result of a write to the client cache *before* the server confirms it, so the UI responds immediately; if the server rejects the write, the client rolls the cache back to the previous snapshot and re-syncs. It trades a small correctness window for perceived latency. It is a *decision about user-visible risk*, not a performance trick.
keyConcepts: The mechanics â€” five moving parts, and all five are required
A complete TanStack Query implementation, including the failure path
Making it robust
Production and operational
"Walk me through the full lifecycle of an optimistic mutation."
"Why is cancelQueries needed in onMutate?"
"How do you roll back correctly when two mutations touch the same list?"
"When would you *not* be optimistic, and what would you show instead?"
"How do you handle an optimistic create when the server assigns the id?"
"What is idempotency and where does it live?"
commonMistakes: Forgetting cancelQueries in onMutate, so a background refetch overwrites the optimistic value and the UI flickers back.
Snapshotting by reference (prev = getQueryData(...)) without structuredClone, so "rollback" restores the object you already mutated.
Rolling back and *not* invalidating, leaving the cache in its pre-mutation (possibly stale) state.
Optimistic create without a clientId, so a retry duplicates.
Optimistic update on a list while a refetchInterval poll is running.
Disabling the button on submit *and* being optimistic â€” the user sees the change but no sign it has not been saved.
Treating isPending from useMutation as per-row; you need per-item pending state (a Set of ids).

optimism without a failure path; rollback without refetch; optimism on irreversible actions; assuming onMutate's returned context survives a component unmount (it does â€” the mutation owns it, which is a feature).

interviewQuestions.text: Explain the mechanics â€” five moving parts, and all five are required and when you would use it.
Explain a complete tanstack query implementation, including the failure path and when you would use it.
Explain making it robust and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: Optimistic updates cut perceived latency to zero and make the UI feel instant; they also introduce a class of bugs that are hard to see â€” a wrong prediction (the server rejects with a validation error you never predicted), a partial apply (two mutations touching the same list concurrently, second snapshot taken *after* the first applied), a stale rollback (snapshot was already stale), and a flash of wrong data for other users if you broadcast optimistically to a shared cache. Mitigations: cancelQueries before mutating, snapshot with structuredClone, always invalidateQueries on settle, and make every optimistic mutation *narrow* â€” one entity, not a whole collection.

topics.title: The state-management decision flowchart
topics.description: A deterministic procedure that, given a piece of state and its requirements, names the tool â€” and justifies it in one sentence. Interviewers use this to test *decision-making under constraints* rather than library recall. The value is in the questions you ask before you pick.
keyConcepts: The flowchart
The three questions that resolve 90% of ambiguity

Who is allowed to write it, and what is the order of writes? One writer â†’ useState. Many writers with no ordering requirement â†’ a store. Many writers where B must not run until A resolves â†’ useReducer or an FSM. Interruption/cancellation requirements â†’ an FSM (4.3.7).

What makes it stale, and who is allowed to refresh it? Nothing (client state, never stale) â†’ store/URL. A TTL â†’ query cache. A server event â†’ query cache invalidated by a subscription. A user action â†’ invalidation with a scope.

What is the blast radius of a wrong value? Cosmetic (hover, animation) â†’ be liberal. Visible and recoverable â†’ be conservative. Money/permissions/irreversible â†’ never optimistic, never client-authoritative.
Decision table for the common interview scenario

**The three questions that resolve 90% of ambiguity.**

1. **Who is allowed to write it, and what is the order of writes?** One writer â†’ `useState`. Many writers with no ordering requirement â†’ a store. Many writers where B must not run until A resolves â†’ `useReducer` or an FSM. Interruption/cancellation requirements â†’ an FSM (4.3.7).
2. **What makes it stale, and who is allowed to refresh it?** Nothing (client state, never stale) â†’ store/URL. A TTL â†’ query cache. A server event â†’ query cache invalidated by a subscription. A user action â†’ invalidation with a scope.
3. **What is the blast radius of a wrong value?** Cosmetic (hover, animation) â†’ be liberal. Visible and recoverable â†’ be conservative. Money/permissions/irreversible â†’ never optimistic, never client-authoritative.

**Decision table for the common interview scenario.** "A team wants one store for everything."

| Requirement | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| "One place to see all client state in DevTools" | Redux Toolkit (devtools) | Time travel + serialisability checks are a real benefit at team size |
| "Minimize boilerplate; small team; 8 screens" | Zustand + TanStack Query | Lowest ceremony, cache delegated to the query layer |
| "Deeply derived state (pricing rules, permissions matrix)" | Jotai derived atoms or MobX `computed` | Automatic dependency graph, memoised, no manual invalidation |
| "A virtualised grid with 100k rows and per-cell subscriptions" | MobX, or a normalised store + virtualisation | Per-property reaction tracking; re-render granularity |
| "Complex async orchestration (uploads, retry, cancellation)" | Redux Toolkit + listener middleware, or XState | Explicit, testable, cancellable; see 4.3.5/4.3.7 |
| "We already have X and it works" | Keep X | Migration cost is the dominant term; only migrate for a named defect |

**A migration playbook** (the real answer to "we have `useState` everywhere, where do we start?"): (1) Inventory every state and classify it with 4.3.1's table â€” this alone surfaces the derived-state duplication bugs. (2) Move all server data to the query layer first; it is the biggest win and the least invasive because components keep the same `data`/`isLoading`/`error` shape. (3) Move shareable view state to the URL. (4) Only then introduce a store for what is left, one slice at a time, keeping the old code path behind a feature flag. (5) Delete the old store when the last consumer migrates; never maintain two sources of truth "temporarily".

**Common mistakes.** Choosing a library before classifying the state; asking "Redux or Zustand?" instead of "what is this state's writer and lifetime?"; putting derived state in the store "for performance" (which is backwards â€” it is the one thing that costs); a store used as a cache; refusing context because "context is slow" without checking whether the problem is an unmemoized `value`; and treating a flowchart as a decision tree that yields one answer when the right answer is often "this is layer 2, not a state-management question at all".

- "How would you migrate this codebase to a query library incrementally?"
- "When would you *add* a store to an app that has none?"
- "What would make you choose MobX over Zustand here?"

Layer 5 (global client state) hygiene rules that apply wherever you land:
  Â· a store must never hold layer 2 or layer 3 (server data)
  Â· one fact â†’ one owner â†’ one write path
  Â· if two stores can write the same key, you have designed a race
  Â· every persisted value is versioned and validated on read
```

**The three questions that resolve 90% of ambiguity.**

1. **Who is allowed to write it, and what is the order of writes?** One writer â†’ `useState`. Many writers with no ordering requirement â†’ a store. Many writers where B must not run until A resolves â†’ `useReducer` or an FSM. Interruption/cancellation requirements â†’ an FSM (4.3.7).
2. **What makes it stale, and who is allowed to refresh it?** Nothing (client state, never stale) â†’ store/URL. A TTL â†’ query cache. A server event â†’ query cache invalidated by a subscription. A user action â†’ invalidation with a scope.
3. **What is the blast radius of a wrong value?** Cosmetic (hover, animation) â†’ be liberal. Visible and recoverable â†’ be conservative. Money/permissions/irreversible â†’ never optimistic, never client-authoritative.

**Decision table for the common interview scenario.** "A team wants one store for everything."

| Requirement | Answer | Why |
|---|---|---|
| "One place to see all client state in DevTools" | Redux Toolkit (devtools) | Time travel + serialisability checks are a real benefit at team size |
| "Minimize boilerplate; small team; 8 screens" | Zustand + TanStack Query | Lowest ceremony, cache delegated to the query layer |
| "Deeply derived state (pricing rules, permissions matrix)" | Jotai derived atoms or MobX `computed` | Automatic dependency graph, memoised, no manual invalidation |
| "A virtualised grid with 100k rows and per-cell subscriptions" | MobX, or a normalised store + virtualisation | Per-property reaction tracking; re-render granularity |
| "Complex async orchestration (uploads, retry, cancellation)" | Redux Toolkit + listener middleware, or XState | Explicit, testable, cancellable; see 4.3.5/4.3.7 |
| "We already have X and it works" | Keep X | Migration cost is the dominant term; only migrate for a named defect |

**A migration playbook** (the real answer to "we have `useState` everywhere, where do we start?"): (1) Inventory every state and classify it with 4.3.1's table â€” this alone surfaces the derived-state duplication bugs. (2) Move all server data to the query layer first; it is the biggest win and the least invasive because components keep the same `data`/`isLoading`/`error` shape. (3) Move shareable view state to the URL. (4) Only then introduce a store for what is left, one slice at a time, keeping the old code path behind a feature flag. (5) Delete the old store when the last consumer migrates; never maintain two sources of truth "temporarily".

**Common mistakes.** Choosing a library before classifying the state; asking "Redux or Zustand?" instead of "what is this state's writer and lifetime?"; putting derived state in the store "for performance" (which is backwards â€” it is the one thing that costs); a store used as a cache; refusing context because "context is slow" without checking whether the problem is an unmemoized `value`; and treating a flowchart as a decision tree that yields one answer when the right answer is often "this is layer 2, not a state-management question at all".

**What an interviewer probes.**
- "Here are 6 pieces of state in my app â€” classify each and justify."
- "Why is 'one store for everything' a red flag?"
- "How would you migrate this codebase to a query library incrementally?"
- "When would you *add* a store to an app that has none?"
- "What would make you choose MobX over Zustand here?"

**Mistakes:** a flowchart without the "what makes it stale" question; assuming a bigger library is a bigger win; skipping the classification step entirely.

groups.title: Data Fetching and Forms
groups.description:
Data Fetching and Forms within React Deep Dive.

---

ðŸŸ¡ Intermediate Â· **Must-know** Â· Prerequisites: 4.1.7 (effects), 4.3.1 (server state)

**Framing.** Data fetching is the largest source of user-perceived latency and the largest source of subtle frontend bugs: duplicate requests, waterfalls, stale data, race conditions, lost writes, and the loading/empty/error matrix nobody designs. The canonical entry for *server-side* rendering and caching is 4.2; this section is the *client* data layer and the form lifecycle. The single organising idea:

> **A data-fetching layer is a cache with a policy.** Policy = when to fetch, when to reuse, when to revalidate, when to throw the data away, and what happens when it fails. Libraries differ only in how expressive that policy language is.

---

topics.title: The data-fetching model: loaders vs effects, and the waterfall problem
topics.description: A *loader* fetches data as part of a navigation or a render's dependency graph, before the consuming UI renders. An *effect* fetches data after the component has committed, imperatively. Almost every bug in this area is a consequence of choosing effects where a loader model was needed.
keyConcepts: Loader vs effect â€” mechanics and consequences
Race conditions. Two rapid param changes â†’ the *first*, slower response can land last and win. Fix with AbortController (cancels the loser) or a request-id guard.
Unnecessary requests on every mount. Back-and-forth navigation re-fetches everything. Fix with a cache and a staleness policy.
Missing cleanup. No abort means a setState after unmount and a wasted connection.
Request cancellation on unmount â€” the same abort controller.
Prefetching: turning navigations warm
Production and operational
"Draw the timeline of an effect-fetch vs a loader-fetch with three dependent requests."
"How do you fix a race between two param changes?"
"What is prefetching and when is it worth it?"
"When is Promise.all the wrong choice?"
"Does aborting a fetch save server work?"
commonMistakes: useEffect(() => { fetch(...); }, []) with no abort and no error branch.
A dependent request guarded by if (!parent) return inside a *separate* effect (a waterfall by construction).
Promise.all where Promise.allSettled was needed because one panel's failure should not blank the page.
Fetching the same resource in a parent and passing it down as a prop *and* having the child fetch it too.
Prefetching on hover with no delay (wastes bandwidth on pass-over links).
Assuming cancellation stops the server work â€” it stops the response being used; say so.
conflating "parallel" with "optimised"; forgetting the unmount cleanup; treating a loading spinner as the only pending state.

tradeoffs: Loaders require a router or framework (harder to unit test in isolation, coupled to navigation), but they make data flow explicit and enable streaming, defer, error boundaries per route, and prefetch-on-navigation. Effects are framework-free and trivially local, and cost you every caching and cancellation property. Query libraries sit between: they own the cache, and they work inside components (so they compose with Suspense and don't force a router).

It owns: a keyed cache of query results, in-flight request deduplication, staleness with staleTime, background revalidation, garbage collection with gcTime, retries with backoff, mutations with a lifecycle, and derived/cache state via select. Its central abstraction is a QueryKey: a stable, serialisable, structural descriptor of a request, hashed to identify a cache entry.

The cache lifecycle â€” the whole thing on one page
staleTime vs gcTime â€” the distinction interviewers always probe
The other features worth knowing in one line each
Infinite queries (useInfiniteQuery, getNextPageParam) â€” 4.4.5.
Suspense: useSuspenseQuery throws a promise; combine with <Suspense> for a route-level skeleton instead of per-hook if (isPending).
queryClient.ensureQueryData / prefetchQuery â€” await the first, fire-and-forget the second; call both in a router loader for a warm navigation.
dehydrate/hydrate â€” move a server cache into the client at hydration, killing a duplicate first fetch.
structuralSharing: false â€” disables deep-equal reuse of *unchanged* parts between refetches; turn it off for very large or non-plain (class/Map) data.
select vs useMemo: select runs inside the cache subscription (narrower); useMemo runs after re-render (wider).

Non-normalised keys: ['list', page, q || undefined, status || undefined] producing two entries for the same logical query.

Forgetting signal in queryFn so cancelled queries still consume bandwidth.

select returning a new array each call inside selectFromResult (loops).

tradeoffs: You get an enormous amount of correct behaviour for ~13 kB gz and a 10-line config, plus DevTools showing every key, its observers, and its timings. You pay a dependency, a learning curve around key design (the #1 source of bugs), cache-invalidation design work, and the fact that a *badly keyed* cache produces subtle duplicate-entity bugs that are hard to see. Compared to SWR: TanStack Query is more explicit and more feature-complete (mutations, infinite queries, devtools with mutation timeline); SWR is smaller, has a simpler mental model, and treats data as immutable-with-mutate (which is closer to React's model).

topics.referenceMarkdown:
ðŸ”´ Advanced Â· **Must-know** Â· Prerequisites: 4.3.9, 4.3.1 (server state)

**Definition:** TanStack Query (formerly React Query) is a *server-state* cache for asynchronous data. It owns: a keyed cache of query results, in-flight request deduplication, staleness with `staleTime`, background revalidation, garbage collection with `gcTime`, retries with backoff, mutations with a lifecycle, and derived/cache state via `select`. Its central abstraction is a **QueryKey**: a stable, serialisable, structural descriptor of a request, hashed to identify a cache entry.

**The mental model to say out loud in an interview.** A query has four states, not two: `pending` (no data yet, fetching), `error` (no data, failed), `success` (data, possibly re-fetching), and `refetching`/`fetching` (data present, network in flight). `isLoading` in v5 means `isPending && isFetching` â€” i.e. *no data yet*. A "refetch" on visible cached data is `isFetching && !isPending`, and that is exactly what `isFetching` is for.

**`queryKey`: a structural contract, the most important 10 lines you will write.**

```tsx
import { useQuery, useQueryClient, QueryClient, queryOptions } from '@tanstack/react-query';

type Filters = { q?: string; status?: 'open' | 'paid'; page?: number };

// (a) Put the key in ONE exported factory. Never hand-write the same array in two components.
export const invoiceKeys = {
  all: ['invoices'] as const,
  lists: () => [...invoiceKeys.all, 'list'] as const,
  list: (filters: Filters) => [...invoiceKeys.lists(), { ...filters }] as const,   // object, not positional args
  details: () => [...invoiceKeys.all, 'detail'] as const,
  detail: (id: string) => [...invoiceKeys.details(), id] as const,
};
// partial matching: invoiceKeys.lists() matches every list key; invoiceKeys.detail(id) matches one.

// (b) Keys are hashed *structurally*, so key order and object key order do not matter:
//   ['list', {a:1, b:2}] === ['list', {b:2, a:1}]   -> same hash.
//   ['list', {a:1}] !== ['list', {a:'1'}]           -> different (values are typed by JSON).
//   ['list', {a:undefined}] vs ['list', {}]          -> {a:undefined} is normalised away by JSON hashing: treat as EQUAL.
//     => Always normalise your key with defaults + omit undefined, or you will create phantom entries.

// (c) queryOptions gives you a typed, reusable "query definition" (key + fn + options) â€” v5 idiom.
const invoiceList = (filters: Filters) =>
  queryOptions({
    queryKey: invoiceKeys.list(filters),
    queryFn: ({ signal }) => api.get<InvoicePage>(`/invoices?${new URLSearchParams(clean(filters))}`, { signal }),
    staleTime: 30_000,
    placeholderData: keepPreviousData,        // paged filter changes keep the old page on screen
  });

export function useInvoiceList(filters: Filters) {
  return useQuery(invoiceList(filters));
}

// (d) select: transform in the cache-read path without breaking sharing. MUST be pure and
//     must return a stable value, or you cause an infinite render loop.
const useFirstInvoice = (filters: Filters) =>
  useQuery({
    ...invoiceList(filters),
    select: (data) => data?.invoices[0] ?? null,          // returns one object: stable across refetches
  });

// (e) subscribe narrowly: the component re-renders only when the fields it names change.
const { invoices, totalCount, isPending, isFetching, isError, refetch } = useQuery({
  ...invoiceList(filters),
  select: (d) => ({ invoices: d?.invoices ?? [], totalCount: d?.totalCount ?? 0 }),  // object literal: safe ONLY because
  // useQuery memoises select output against the raw data reference; the raw data is stable between refetches.
  // (That memoisation is why select is safe and useStore(selector) in a plain store is not.)
});

// (f) enabled: the declarative "not yet" â€” no fake filter values, no effect.
const useInvoice = (id: string | null) =>
  useQuery({ ...invoiceKeys.detail(id ?? ''), queryFn: () => api.get<Invoice>(`/invoices/${id}`), enabled: !!id });
```

**`queryKey`: a structural contract, the most important 10 lines you will write.**

  details: () => [...invoiceKeys.all, 'detail'] as const,
  detail: (id: string) => [...invoiceKeys.details(), id] as const,
};
// partial matching: invoiceKeys.lists() matches every list key; invoiceKeys.detail(id) matches one.

// (b) Keys are hashed *structurally*, so key order and object key order do not matter:
//   ['list', {a:1, b:2}] === ['list', {b:2, a:1}]   -> same hash.
//   ['list', {a:1}] !== ['list', {a:'1'}]           -> different (values are typed by JSON).
//   ['list', {a:undefined}] vs ['list', {}]          -> {a:undefined} is normalised away by JSON hashing: treat as EQUAL.
//     => Always normalise your key with defaults + omit undefined, or you will create phantom entries.

// (c) queryOptions gives you a typed, reusable "query definition" (key + fn + options) â€” v5 idiom.

    queryKey: invoiceKeys.list(filters),
    queryFn: ({ signal }) => api.get<InvoicePage>(`/invoices?${new URLSearchParams(clean(filters))}`, { signal }),
    staleTime: 30_000,
    placeholderData: keepPreviousData,        // paged filter changes keep the old page on screen
  });

  return useQuery(invoiceList(filters));

//     must return a stable value, or you cause an infinite render loop.

    ...invoiceList(filters),
    select: (data) => data?.invoices[0] ?? null,          // returns one object: stable across refetches

topics.title: SWR and the compare-and-swap revalidation model
topics.description: SWR is a data-fetching hook built on stale-while-revalidate: serve cached data immediately, then revalidate in the background; accept a newer response only if it is actually newer (compare-and-swap). Its API surface is three functions â€” useSWR, mutate, and useSWRConfig â€” and its philosophy is that data is immutable and cache writes are explicit, which matches React's model closely.

Conditional fetching and dependent keys
Pagination and infinite queries in SWR

"Why does SWR dedupe requests?"

commonMistakes: revalidateOnFocus: false globally "to reduce requests" and then shipping stale data on every tab switch.
Mutating a cached object in place (data.name = x) instead of going through mutate â€” no re-render, no cache coherence.
Not passing keepPreviousData on a param change, so every id change flashes a skeleton.
useSWRInfinite's getKey returning a URL for pageIndex before checking previousPageData (an extra request and a flash of undefined).
Expecting mutate(fn) to be a rollback mechanism for arbitrary errors (it is a CAS write; rollbackOnError is the option you want).
Assuming SWR aborts in-flight fetches â€” it dedupes but cancellation needs AbortController in the fetcher keyed off a request id.
treating SWR's cache as mutable; importing from swr/_internal without acknowledging it; conflating deduping with cancellation.

tradeoffs: SWR's small surface is its main feature *and* its main limitation: fewer escape hatches means "I need to know exactly when this refetches" sometimes requires reaching into internals (swr/_internal), which is a smell you should name in an interview rather than do casually. SWR's implicit revalidation on focus can also surprise you (three tabs on the same app all refetch on focus). TanStack Query's explicitness costs more code but makes invalidation *reviewable* â€” a real advantage at scale and in code review.

topics.title: Mutations, invalidation, optimistic updates, and rollback
topics.description: A mutation is an intentional write to the server. Unlike a query (implicitly re-fetched by anything), a mutation only runs when you ask for it, and its aftermath â€” which caches are now wrong, and what the user sees while it runs â€” is an explicit design decision. In TanStack Query that decision is the useMutation lifecycle; in Redux it is createAsyncThunk + invalidation; in a router it is an action.

Rolling back to a snapshot taken *after* another optimistic write. Treating 4xx like 5xx: a validation error should show the server's field errors, not "something went wrong", and must not roll back to a state that is now obviously wrong. No idempotency key on a payment. Optimistic update on a resource other users read (you are now lying to your own cache about shared data). Firing mutate from a useEffect (an event-driven operation belongs in an event handler).

topics.title: Pagination: offset vs cursor, infinite queries, bidirectional scroll
topics.description: Pagination is the policy for reading a bounded window of a large collection. Two families exist: offset pagination (?page=2 / ?offset=50&limit=20, computed by the database) and cursor (keyset) pagination (?after=<opaque> / ?before=<opaque>, walking a sort key). Infinite scroll is a UI pattern that repeatedly extends a cursor-paginated collection; infinite *queries* are the cache structure that supports it.
keyConcepts: The mechanics and the failure each family has
Bidirectional scroll â€” the part most implementations skip
maxPages and the memory model
Offset pagination done properly
Production and operational

Every cursor must be validated server-side and scoped to the filter set (a cursor from filter A is nonsense for filter B) â€” encode the filter hash into the cursor and reject mismatches, or you get leaked pages.
Log the number of pages fetched per session; a long-tail tail means maxPages is wrong or the sentinel margin is too small.

Watch the DB: OFFSET 400000 shows up as a sequential scan; a missing composite index on (created_at, id) shows up as slow cursor queries. Cursor pagination is only fast if the index exists *in the sort order*.
Track "duplicate row seen" rate in analytics as a data-integrity signal â€” offset pagination on a mutating table shows up in product metrics as engagement oddities nobody can explain.
"Offset vs cursor: give the exact failure of each."
"How do you handle a post inserted while the user pages?"
"How do you load older messages when scrolling up?"
commonMistakes: Infinite scroll as the only path to content. No maxPages. Forgetting to dedupe by id. Offset pagination on a mutating feed. Cursor sort key not being unique. No "Load more" button. Restoring scroll by pixel offset after a prepend (it jumps). Using the sentinel with rootMargin: '0px' and a fast scroll, causing request storms â€” use a margin and a isFetching guard.
assuming infinite scroll is free; keepPreviousData forgotten on page changes; a cursor that leaks filter state; no dedupe.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain the mechanics and the failure each family has and when you would use it.
Explain bidirectional scroll â€” the part most implementations skip and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: Cursor pagination is the correct choice for correctness and index efficiency, and it costs you page numbers and total counts (both need either a second query or an approximate count â€” say "1,200+" rather than an exact number, which is what good products do). Infinite scroll removes pagination UI but harms: find-in-page, returning to a position, the back button, and accessibility (no page boundaries). The senior answer is that infinite scroll is a *UI* decision that should be paired with (a) a URL-representable anchor for restoration, (b) a keyboard-reachable "Load more", and (c) maxPages + virtualisation so memory is bounded. Server-side aggregation for huge tables beats client pagination entirely: if a user only sees 25 rows, never fetch 100k.

topics.title: Polling vs WebSockets vs SSE for live data
topics.description: Three ways to learn that remote data changed. Polling asks on a timer. Server-Sent Events (SSE) is a one-way serverâ†’client stream over HTTP. WebSockets are a bidirectional, persistent, upgradeable protocol with framing. The choice is about *push capability vs* complexity, cost, and failure modes â€” and it should be driven by how fresh the data must be.
keyConcepts: The comparison, honestly
Choosing
Does the user need to *see* changes without doing anything? If no â†’ no live data at all; use invalidation on focus (4.4.11). Most "live" requirements are actually "when I come back, it is correct".
Is the staleness tolerance measured in minutes? â†’ polling with an interval above the tolerance, paused when hidden. 99% of dashboards, admin panels, and order lists.
Seconds, and one-way (server tells client)? â†’ SSE. Notifications, job progress, live scores, presence, "someone commented".
Seconds, and the client must talk (typing indicators, subscriptions per entity, presence)? â†’ WebSocket, and accept the operational cost.
Multi-user concurrent editing â†’ WebSocket + CRDT/OT (4.6.11.5), and acknowledge this is a multi-month project, not a feature.
Production and operational

Every transport needs a resync path. Polling: none (the next tick is the resync). SSE: Last-Event-ID replay. WebSocket: since=lastSeq on reconnect plus a GET /messages?since= reconciliation. Never assume the stream is complete.
Detect half-open connections: ping/pong for WS, a comment frame for SSE, and a server-side idle timeout. A TCP connection that looks open can be dead for hours behind a NAT.

Broadcast from the server layer, not from request handlers: after a transaction commits, publish to Redis/NATS/Kafka; the WS/SSE gateway subscribes. Otherwise you need N socket servers (one per app instance) and users on different instances see different data â€” the classic "works locally, stale in production" bug.
Rate-limit the *outbound* stream per connection (coalesce updates: a row changing 100Ã—/s should send the latest value every 100 ms, not 100 events).
commonMistakes: EventSource closed in onerror (you turn a self-healing stream into a dead one). lastSeq in the effect deps (constant reconnects). No jitter on reconnect (thundering herd on recovery). Assuming SSE works behind nginx without disabling buffering. Polling with an interval *below* staleTime (double requests). Treating a WS message as truth and rendering it directly, bypassing the cache (you now have two sources of truth and no invalidation).
"WebSocket for everything"; closing an EventSource in onerror; no resync after reconnect; polling in a hidden tab.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain the comparison, honestly and when you would use it.
