tradeoffs: Polling is trivially reliable and CDN/proxy-friendly, but its cost scales as clients Ã— (60 / interval) requests and it cannot express "this row changed"; at 5 s across 10k clients that is 120k requests/min â€” at which point you want SSE plus a change-feed endpoint. SSE is nearly free at idle and reconnects itself, but it is one-way, text-only, and depends on proxy configuration (buffering is the classic bug: you send events and nothing arrives until the buffer fills). WebSockets are the most capable and the most expensive to operate: connection draining on deploy, sticky sessions behind a load balancer or a broker for fan-out, per-connection memory, heartbeats to detect half-open connections, and mobile networks that drop connections constantly â€” so reconnect-with-backoff and a resync query are mandatory, not optional.

topics.title: React Hook Form and Formik: uncontrolled-first philosophy
topics.description: A form library's job is to own values, validation, submission, error mapping, and the *pending* state, with as few re-renders as possible. React Hook Form (RHF) is uncontrolled-first: it reads values from the DOM through refs on submit (and on demand), so typing causes zero React re-renders. Formik is controlled-first: every change is a setState, so typing re-renders the form (it mitigates this with validateOnChange toggles and deferring validation).

The philosophy, stated precisely
What both libraries give you that hand-rolled forms do not

Server errors overwriting client state or vice versa. setSubmitting(false) missing in Formik's catch path. Keys by index in useFieldArray (f.id exists for a reason). Losing focus on every validation change because the whole form remounts (missing key). Clearing a field's error before the user has interacted with it.
reaching for a library to validate one input; re-rendering the form on every keystroke; treating client validation as a security boundary.

tradeoffs: Validation timing is the real decision. mode: 'onChange' is hostile (errors while typing); onBlur is decent; onTouched is the best default; onSubmit is the most accessible (errors appear after an explicit attempt) and is what progressive-enhancement forms do. Use mode: 'onBlur' + reValidateMode: 'onChange'.
Async validation needs cancellation â€” a uniqueness check on email. RHF handles it; hand-rolled does not, and you get a stale "email is taken" for the previous value.
Server errors are not client errors. A 422 body of { email: "already taken" } must be mapped to field errors, not shown as a form-level toast. Put the mapping in one function (above) and test it.

Never disable submit based on isValid in RHF without knowing isValid means "validated at least once" â€” with mode: 'onTouched' a pristine form reports false, so the button is disabled until the user touches a field, which looks broken. Use isSubmitting for the disabled state and let validation handle correctness.
Password/autofill: autoComplete="new-password", autoComplete="email", correct inputMode, and type="email" â€” this is a conversion and accessibility problem that no library solves for you.
Unsaved-changes warning: isDirty && !isSubmitting â†’ beforeunload guard plus a router navigation blocker.

Multi-step forms: one schema per step (partial via .pick()), keep all values in one form instance, and validate only the current step's fields with trigger(fields); a wizard is a great XState candidate if steps have guarded transitions (4.3.7).

topics.title: Schema validation with Zod and Yup, shared client/server schemas
topics.description: A schema is a declarative, executable specification of the shape of valid data that also (a) validates at runtime, (b) infers a TypeScript type, and (c) can produce a human-readable error *path*. Zod and Yup are the two dominant implementations. The high-value pattern is one schema module imported by both the client form and the server handler, so the contract cannot drift.
keyConcepts: Zod vs Yup, mechanically
When to validate, in which layer
Why the client copy is not a security control
Structural rules you must encode deliberately

z.object strips unknown keys (v3) â€” a client sending { role: 'owner', isAdmin: true } has isAdmin silently dropped. That is usually *desirable* (mass-assignment defence), but use .strict() when you want a loud failure instead of silence.

Coercion is a security-relevant decision. z.coerce.number() turns "" into 0 and null into 0. For numbers that must be present, use z.number() and validate the string first, or use z.preprocess with an explicit empty check. Same for z.coerce.boolean(): "false" coerces to true in JS. This is a classic real bug.
z.string() does not trim. .trim() is a transform; order matters (z.string().trim().min(1)).

Optional vs nullable are different types. z.string().optional() accepts undefined but not null; .nullable() accepts null. Omitting the modifier is the most common source of "why does my optional field fail validation".
Dates: validate as strings with a format check at the boundary, then convert to Date/Temporal inside â€” never accept a Date from JSON.parse (it arrives as a string).
Enums vs literals: z.enum([...]) gives a union type and rejects unknown values; that is exactly what you want for a role.
partial() vs a new schema: .partial() is for updates where every field is optional; then remember that undefined means "don't change" while null must be a separate path.
File and URL fields: validate on the *server* with content sniffing and size limits; a client File type check is a hint, not a control.
commonMistakes: Validating on the server with a *different* shape than the client (the drift this pattern exists to prevent). z.coerce.boolean() silently inverting "false". Using .optional() where the API sends null. Only validating in the client. Showing a generic "invalid input" instead of mapping field errors. A schema per component so the same field is validated three ways. Leaking server policy details to the client and then treating them as enforced.
two schemas that drift; coercion without checking; stripping unknown keys when you wanted rejection; schema errors surfaced as one big red banner.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain zod vs yup, mechanically and when you would use it.

Explain why the client copy is not a security control and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: One shared schema means one place to change the contract, but it also couples your client bundle to the server contract (a heavy schema with a big enum costs bundle size) and it forces you to decide what *not* to share (password policy details, rate limits). The pragmatic split: share *shape* and *user-facing* messages; keep *policy* (rate limits, permission, uniqueness) on the server. Zod v4 improved tree-shaking via a modular core (zod/mini) and added better error maps; if bundle size matters, check the current docs rather than assuming v3 behaviour â€” and the same for z.email() (v4 made top-level string formats, z.string().email() is deprecated in v4). Always verify against the version you have installed.

topics.title: File upload UX: progress, previews, multipart, presigned URLs
topics.description: File upload is not a form field; it is a resumable, observable, retryable, cancellable transfer that a user is watching. The design problem has five parts: the UX states (idle â†’ validating â†’ uploading with progress â†’ processing â†’ done/failed), the transport (single POST vs multipart vs direct-to-object-storage), the preview, the queue (concurrency), and the failure/retry path.
keyConcepts: Why you cannot use fetch for progress
The transport decision â€” this is the real engineering
Previews â€” the part that looks easy and is not
The upload queue UX
"Why can't you get upload progress with fetch?"
"Presigned vs multipart: when and why?"
"What must the server do after a presigned upload, and why?"
"How do you make a 2 GB upload resumable?"
"How do you avoid leaking memory with previews?"
"What are the security risks of client uploads?"
commonMistakes: fetch for a progress bar (no progress events). Revoking an object URL while it is still displayed. Trusting file.type server-side. Presigning without ownership scoping or with a 24-hour expiry. Uploading through the app server for multi-GB files. No concurrency limit (20 parallel 100 MB uploads). Announcing every percent to a live region. Losing the queue on refresh.
URL.createObjectURL without revoke; unbounded concurrency; no server-side verification of the uploaded object; assuming a presigned PUT means the file is validated.

Explain the transport decision â€” this is the real engineering and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: Direct-to-storage saves the most money of anything in this section. A 2 GB/day video product that proxies uploads pays double egress and needs serverless with huge timeouts; presigned PUTs make the app server stateless.

Presigned URLs are capabilities: short expiry, exact key, exact content type, pinned content length, and a quarantine/ prefix that only your worker can promote. Never let the client choose the key freely (path traversal, overwriting other users' objects, serving XSS from your domain).
Timeouts and proxies: an upload through your server dies at 30â€“60 s on most ingress. That alone is the reason to move large uploads off your server.

Resumability requires persisting { key, uploadId, parts: [{ PartNumber, ETag }] } in IndexedDB; on resume, call ListParts and upload only what is missing. This is a real feature users notice on mobile.

Never trust File.type â€” it is whatever the OS reported, and on some platforms it is empty. Sniff magic bytes server-side (file-type), re-encode images, strip EXIF, and transcode video (an uploaded "video" can be a 4 GB decompression bomb).

Serving uploads: serve user content from a *different domain* than your app (so an XSS in an HTML upload cannot touch your session), with Content-Disposition: attachment for non-media, a strict Content-Type, and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.
Cost/UX: for large files, show an estimated time, run uploads while the user does something else, and support paste-from-clipboard (onPaste) and drag-from-Finder.
Mobile: capture="environment" for camera, accept="image/*" for the picker (accepts HEIC on iOS), and remember iOS may downscale the video before it reaches you.

topics.title: Loading, empty, and error states as a first-class design problem
topics.description: Every asynchronous surface has at least five states, not two: *initial loading* (nothing on screen yet), *refreshing* (data present, new data coming), *empty* (the request succeeded and there is nothing), *partial* (some parts failed / some data missing), and *error* (the request failed). UIs that only handle loading + data are incomplete, and the missing states are what users report as bugs.

Loading strategies, and the threshold that decides between them

A full-page spinner for a 200 ms sidebar. role="alert" on the loading container (announces constantly). Skeletons with a different layout from the content. A retry button that refetches with the same broken parameters. No error correlation id shown to support.

topics.title: Cache invalidation strategies and the stale-write problem
topics.description: Invalidation is the policy that decides *which cached reads become wrong after a write, and how they learn about it*. The stale-write problem is the specific failure where two writes race â€” or where a write succeeds but the cache still shows the old value â€” and it is the reason "just invalidate everything" is a temporary answer, not a strategy.
keyConcepts: The four sources of cache invalidation
A strategy matrix
The stale-write problem, precisely
Making staleness visible and bounded
A concrete, defensible policy you can present in an interview
Production and operational
Log invalidations in development: wrap invalidateQueries in a helper that console.logs the key and the caller. Half of "my data is stale" bugs become obvious immediately.
Test the invalidation graph: for each mutation, a unit test that asserts the expected keys are invalidated and that an unrelated key is *not*. This is the cheapest high-value test in a data layer.

Alert on refetch volume (requests per user-minute). A sudden rise usually means a refetch loop: refetchInterval too low, an invalidate inside an effect, or staleTime: 0 with refetchOnFocus on a route users tab between constantly.
Clear the cache on identity changes: logout, tenant switch, permission downgrade (queryClient.clear()), and on a 401 broadcast from another tab (via BroadcastChannel).
Bound the cache: track queryCache.getAll().length and total serialised size; set gcTime deliberately for high-cardinality keys.
Never trust the client cache for authorisation. It is a UX optimisation over server checks (4.6.9).
commonMistakes: Invalidating with a key that matches nothing. Invalidating in a useEffect (an infinite refetch loop). Not cancelling queries before an optimistic write. staleTime: Infinity plus a new read path that forgets to invalidate. Forgetting that a queryKey missing a filter makes two cache entries for one logical view. React Query's refetchOnMount default being true while assuming it means "always refetch".
invalidateQueries from an effect; no key discipline; treating the cache as authoritative for permissions; rolling back without refetching.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain the four sources of cache invalidation and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: Broad invalidation is simple and correct and costs a request storm that grows with your app â€” it is a *deferred architecture bill*. Precise invalidation is efficient and requires a mental model of every dependent read, which is real ongoing cost and is invisible in code review (a new component with a new query key silently becomes a missed dependent). Push invalidation is the most correct and the most operationally expensive (4.4.6). staleTime: Infinity is the best performance and the worst failure mode (permanent wrongness from a missed invalidation) â€” reserve it for data you fully own.

groups.description:
Routing Strategies within React Deep Dive.

---

ðŸŸ¡ Intermediate Â· **Must-know** Â· Prerequisites: 4.1.16 (portals), 4.2 (meta-frameworks), 4.3.8 (URL state)

**Framing.** A router is four things at once: (1) a **matcher** turning a URL into a component tree, (2) a **navigation model** with history semantics, (3) a **boundary system** for code splitting, error handling, and data loading, and (4) a **contract with the server** (what a deep link must render, what a crawler sees, what a 404 is). Most routing bugs are in (2) or (4) â€” history semantics and the server contract â€” while most routing *discussion* is about (1), which is the easy part.

---

It costs: a real dependency, an initial bundle that must include the router, SEO and first-paint concerns for public pages (solved by SSR/SSG â€” 4.2.2), history-semantics bugs, and the requirement that a server rewrite every unknown path to index.html so a deep link works (the single most common deployment mistake: GET /invoices/42 â†’ 404 because the server does not know the app is an SPA).

topics.title: Hash vs history mode
topics.description: Two URL schemes. History mode uses real paths (/invoices/42) with the History API. Hash mode puts the route inside the fragment (/#/invoices/42), which is never sent to the server and fires hashchange instead of popstate.
keyConcepts: The decisive technical differences (beyond aesthetics)

Server visibility. The fragment is never sent in an HTTP request. So: no server-side auth check on #/admin, no server-side redirect of #/login?next=/billing, no per-route HTTP caching, no ability to give a deep link its own server-rendered payload. If you need any of these, hash routing is the wrong tool.

When the fragment is available to client code. It arrives *after* the document loads, so a hash router needs a hydration-safe read (useEffect/useLayoutEffect, not render) or you get a flash of the wrong route. History mode has the path from the first byte.

Failure mode. History mode fails loudly if the server rewrite is missing (a 404 on every deep link). Hash mode "just works" anywhere â€” which is why it dominated the pre-2015 era and why some internal tools still use it.
Analytics. pageview tools that read location.pathname see one page forever in hash mode; you must parse the hash yourself and fire synthetic pageviews.
Where hash routing is still the right answer

Non-SPA contexts where you cannot configure the server: opening file:// pages, embedding inside an iframe served by another team, a static host where the fallback is fixed, a browser extension, a desktop app using a custom protocol.

Fragments used as *data* or *state*, not as routes: OAuth implicit-grant return values (#access_token=... â€” legacy, do not build new flows on this; use PKCE, PHASE 7), or a client-side deep-link target for a native app (myapp://open/#/invoice/42).
In-page anchors (#section) â€” the ordinary, boring, correct use of the fragment.
When it is the wrong answer

topics.referenceMarkdown:
ðŸŸ¢ Beginner Â· **Must-know** Â· Prerequisites: 4.5.1

**Definition:** Two URL schemes. **History mode** uses real paths (`/invoices/42`) with the History API. **Hash mode** puts the route inside the fragment (`/#/invoices/42`), which is never sent to the server and fires `hashchange` instead of `popstate`.

```
History mode                             Hash mode
https://app.example.com/invoices/42      https://app.example.com/#/invoices/42
  â”œâ”€ server sees the full path             â”œâ”€ server sees ONLY /  (the fragment is never transmitted)
  â”œâ”€ needs SPA fallback rewrite            â”œâ”€ no rewrite needed: every route is the same document
  â”œâ”€ needs server cooperation for auth/    â”œâ”€ auth in the fragment is invisible to the server
  â”‚  redirects (fragment arrives late)     â”‚
  â”œâ”€ SEO: crawlers see real URLs           â”œâ”€ SEO: poor; modern crawlers partly cope, but the canonical
  â”‚                                          URL is /#/, so unique-content indexing is unreliable
  â”œâ”€ pretty, shareable, cacheable          â”œâ”€ ugly, but bulletproof
  â””â”€ popstate                             â””â”€ hashchange
```

**The decisive technical differences (beyond aesthetics).**

1. **Server visibility.** The fragment is never sent in an HTTP request. So: no server-side auth check on `#/admin`, no server-side redirect of `#/login?next=/billing`, no per-route HTTP caching, no ability to give a deep link its own server-rendered payload. If you need any of these, hash routing is the wrong tool.
2. **When the fragment is available to client code.** It arrives *after* the document loads, so a hash router needs a hydration-safe read (`useEffect`/`useLayoutEffect`, not render) or you get a flash of the wrong route. History mode has the path from the first byte.
3. **Failure mode.** History mode fails loudly if the server rewrite is missing (a 404 on every deep link). Hash mode "just works" anywhere â€” which is why it dominated the pre-2015 era and why some internal tools still use it.
4. **Analytics.** `pageview` tools that read `location.pathname` see one page forever in hash mode; you must parse the hash yourself and fire synthetic pageviews.

```tsx
// Reading hash state without a hydration flash (and building the base path correctly).
function useHashRoute(): string {
  const [path, setPath] = useState('/');
  useEffect(() => {
    const read = () => setPath(window.location.hash.slice(1) || '/');
    read();
    window.addEventListener('hashchange', read);
    return () => window.removeEventListener('hashchange', read);
  }, []);
  return path;
}
// hash links: <a href="#/invoices/42"> â€” and NEVER a hash for in-page anchors in the same app
// ("#section" and "#/route" collide). Pick one or the other, or use ?section=.
```

**Where hash routing is still the right answer.**
- **Non-SPA contexts where you cannot configure the server**: opening `file://` pages, embedding inside an iframe served by another team, a static host where the fallback is fixed, a browser extension, a desktop app using a custom protocol.
- **Fragments used as *data* or *state*, not as routes**: OAuth implicit-grant return values (`#access_token=...` â€” legacy, do not build new flows on this; use PKCE, PHASE 7), or a client-side deep-link target for a native app (`myapp://open/#/invoice/42`).
- **In-page anchors** (`#section`) â€” the ordinary, boring, correct use of the fragment.

**When it is the wrong answer.** Public or marketing pages that must be indexed or share preview cards (Slack/Discord unfurls read the URL). Anything with server-side authentication or per-route redirects. Any multi-page app where URLs appear in support tickets, emails, or QR codes (a hash URL with an escaped token is unauditable and ugly in print). Anything behind a corporate proxy that strips fragments from logs.

**Trade-offs summary.** History mode: the correct default. Hash mode: less infrastructure coupling, worse semantics. The migration from hash to history is usually "never", because URLs are already in the wild â€” plan for a redirect map if you ever migrate (`/#/invoices/42` â†’ `/invoices/42` via a small script on the hash page).

topics.bodyMarkdown:
ðŸŸ¢ Beginner Â· **Must-know** Â· Prerequisites: 4.5.1

**Definition:** Two URL schemes. **History mode** uses real paths (`/invoices/42`) with the History API. **Hash mode** puts the route inside the fragment (`/#/invoices/42`), which is never sent to the server and fires `hashchange` instead of `popstate`.

```
History mode                             Hash mode
https://app.example.com/invoices/42      https://app.example.com/#/invoices/42
  â”œâ”€ server sees the full path             â”œâ”€ server sees ONLY /  (the fragment is never transmitted)
  â”œâ”€ needs SPA fallback rewrite            â”œâ”€ no rewrite needed: every route is the same document
  â”œâ”€ needs server cooperation for auth/    â”œâ”€ auth in the fragment is invisible to the server
  â”‚  redirects (fragment arrives late)     â”‚
  â”œâ”€ SEO: crawlers see real URLs           â”œâ”€ SEO: poor; modern crawlers partly cope, but the canonical
  â”‚                                          URL is /#/, so unique-content indexing is unreliable
  â”œâ”€ pretty, shareable, cacheable          â”œâ”€ ugly, but bulletproof
  â””â”€ popstate                             â””â”€ hashchange
```

**The decisive technical differences (beyond aesthetics).**

1. **Server visibility.** The fragment is never sent in an HTTP request. So: no server-side auth check on `#/admin`, no server-side redirect of `#/login?next=/billing`, no per-route HTTP caching, no ability to give a deep link its own server-rendered payload. If you need any of these, hash routing is the wrong tool.
2. **When the fragment is available to client code.** It arrives *after* the document loads, so a hash router needs a hydration-safe read (`useEffect`/`useLayoutEffect`, not render) or you get a flash of the wrong route. History mode has the path from the first byte.
3. **Failure mode.** History mode fails loudly if the server rewrite is missing (a 404 on every deep link). Hash mode "just works" anywhere â€” which is why it dominated the pre-2015 era and why some internal tools still use it.
4. **Analytics.** `pageview` tools that read `location.pathname` see one page forever in hash mode; you must parse the hash yourself and fire synthetic pageviews.

```tsx
// Reading hash state without a hydration flash (and building the base path correctly).
function useHashRoute(): string {
  const [path, setPath] = useState('/');
  useEffect(() => {
    const read = () => setPath(window.location.hash.slice(1) || '/');
    read();
    window.addEventListener('hashchange', read);
    return () => window.removeEventListener('hashchange', read);
  }, []);
  return path;
}
// hash links: <a href="#/invoices/42"> â€” and NEVER a hash for in-page anchors in the same app
// ("#section" and "#/route" collide). Pick one or the other, or use ?section=.
```

**Where hash routing is still the right answer.**
- **Non-SPA contexts where you cannot configure the server**: opening `file://` pages, embedding inside an iframe served by another team, a static host where the fallback is fixed, a browser extension, a desktop app using a custom protocol.
- **Fragments used as *data* or *state*, not as routes**: OAuth implicit-grant return values (`#access_token=...` â€” legacy, do not build new flows on this; use PKCE, PHASE 7), or a client-side deep-link target for a native app (`myapp://open/#/invoice/42`).
- **In-page anchors** (`#section`) â€” the ordinary, boring, correct use of the fragment.

**When it is the wrong answer.** Public or marketing pages that must be indexed or share preview cards (Slack/Discord unfurls read the URL). Anything with server-side authentication or per-route redirects. Any multi-page app where URLs appear in support tickets, emails, or QR codes (a hash URL with an escaped token is unauditable and ugly in print). Anything behind a corporate proxy that strips fragments from logs.

**Trade-offs summary.** History mode: the correct default. Hash mode: less infrastructure coupling, worse semantics. The migration from hash to history is usually "never", because URLs are already in the wild â€” plan for a redirect map if you ever migrate (`/#/invoices/42` â†’ `/invoices/42` via a small script on the hash page).

**Common mistakes.** Using hash routing "because it's simpler" on a public app. Expecting the server to see `#` values. Hash URLs for routing *and* anchors in the same app. Missing the hydration flash when reading `location.hash` during render.

**What an interviewer probes.**
- "What does the server see in a hash URL?"
- "When would you legitimately choose hash routing?"
- "What breaks with SEO and with auth redirects?"
- "How do you avoid the flash when reading the hash?"

**Mistakes:** hash routing for a public app; reading `location.hash` during render; assuming server-side auth works with a fragment.

Optional catch-all segments exist so `/docs` and `/docs/getting-started/install` match one route without an ambiguous second definition. **The matching algorithm, and why route order matters.** A router matches *all* the candidate routes, ranks them by specificity, and picks the most specific. Ranking rules: more static segments beat dynamic, dynamic beats splat, longer static prefixes beat shorter, and an optional segment makes a route *less* specific than its non-optional twin. ```ts // React Router 6/7 route config. Dynamic = ':id'; splat = '*'; optional catch-all = ':lang?/*path'. const routes = [ { path: '/', element: }, { path: '/invoices', element: }, { path: '/invoices/new', element: }, // static wins over /invoices/:id { path: '/invoices/:id', element: , loader: invoiceLoader }, // params.id { path: '/invoices/:id/edit', element: }, { path: '/invoices/:id/attachments/*', element: }, // params['*'] = 'a/b/c.pdf' { path: '/docs', element: }, { path: '/docs/:lang?/*path', element: }, // matches /docs AND /docs/fr/getting-started { path: '/files/*', element: }, { path: '*', element: }, // LAST, or it eats everything ]; createBrowserRouter(routes); ``` ``` Ranking table (React Router ranks and sorts; you rarely rely on order, but you should understand it): /invoices/new static 1 dynamic-less segment, fully static â†’ wins over /invoices/:id /invoices/:id/edit 3 segments with 1 dynamic /invoices/:id 2 segments with 1 dynamic /invoices/:id/* splat /:lang?/docs optional dynamic /* catch-all â†’ always least specific ``` **Why optional catch-all exists.** Without it, `/docs` and `/docs/a/b/c` need two route definitions whose patterns overlap, so `/docs` renders through the catch-all route with `path === ''`. With `:lang?/*path`, one route handles both, and `path` tells the component whether it is a directory index (`''`) or a document (`'getting-started/install'`). Next.js's equivalent is an optional catch-all folder `[...slug]`; Remix/React Router's is `:lang?/*path`. ```tsx // Reading params, including splats, and validating them at the boundary (4.4.8). import { useParams, useMatch, useLocation } from 'react-router-dom'; import { z } from 'z'; const InvoiceParams = z.object({ id: z.string().uuid('Not an invoice id') }); export function InvoiceDetail() { const params = useParams(); const parsed = InvoiceParams.safeParse(params); const location = useLocation(); if (!parsed.success) return ; // a malformed URL is a 400, not a crash const { id } = parsed.data; // Splat: '/invoices/x/attachments/2024/q3/report.pdf' â†’ params['*'] === '2024/q3/report.pdf' // Decode each segment yourself; do not assume the server encoded it. const segments = (params['*'] ?? '').split('/').filter(Boolean).map(decodeURIComponent); // Nesting depth via useMatch: how deep am I? Useful for breadcrumbs and analytics. const matches = useMatch('/invoices/:id/attachments/*'); // null if not on that route return

Invoice {id}

; } ``` **Nesting mechanics.** Two distinct kinds of nesting, often confused: - **Layout nesting** (shared chrome persists): a parent route element renders ``. In Next.js App Router this is `layout.tsx`; the parent does **not** re-render on child navigation, which is the performance win. - **Path nesting** (the child path is *relative to* the parent): `children: [{ path: 'edit', ... }]` inside `path: '/invoices/:id'`. Flatten when the "layout" is only styling (a `

Normalise (`..`, duplicate slashes, absolute paths) and never pass it to `fs` unchecked. - **`basename`** for apps served from a subpath (`/admin/app`) â€” set it once on the router; forgetting it breaks every asset-relative URL. **Common mistakes.** Catch-all before specific routes. topics.title: Data loaders and actions in the routing layer
topics.description: A loader is a function the router runs *before* rendering a route, receiving the request (params, search, request object) and returning data for that route. An action is the same contract for mutations: it receives submitted data, performs the write, and returns a result. Both are the router's data layer, and both are the place where "fetch before render" becomes a framework feature instead of a useEffect.
keyConcepts: The loader contract, end to end
Subtle but important mechanics
Next.js equivalents
Production and operational
"What is the difference between a loader and an action?"
"How do loaders avoid waterfalls?"
"What is defer for?"
"When does a loader re-run, and how do you stop it?"
"Why would you use a query library inside a route that has a loader?"
commonMistakes: Calling your API without forwarding auth headers (redirect loops). Using useEffect + fetch inside a route component anyway. Expecting useNavigation().state to identify which route. Revalidating on every query-string change. Loaders that ignore shouldRevalidate and hammer the API. Throwing new Error instead of a Response for expected states (everything becomes a 500).
mixing the two data models without a rule; unauthenticated loader fetches; no shouldRevalidate tuning.

interviewQuestions.text: Explain the loader contract, end to end and when you would use it.
Explain subtle but important mechanics and when you would use it.
Explain next.js equivalents and when you would use it.
Explain production and operational and when you would use it.
Explain "what is the difference between a loader and an action?" and when you would use it.

tradeoffs: Loaders: explicit, no waterfall, SSR-capable, progressive enhancement, and impossible to render with the wrong data (fetch-before-render is a *guarantee*, not a convention). Costs: you must learn a second data model; loaders run on *every* navigation unless you tune shouldRevalidate; data is not shared with non-router components (a modal rendered outside the route tree cannot use useLoaderData); and client-side-only caching of loader data requires extra work (dehydrate/hydrate, 4.4.2). Effects/queries: better caching and sharing, worse guarantees. The honest senior position: *use the router's loader for the route's data (it is the only thing that can SSR and stream it correctly), and use a query cache for incremental and shared client-side data.*

topics.title: Route guards and protected routes with auth
topics.description: A route guard is code that decides whether the current navigation may proceed. The critical, security-relevant distinction: client and router guards are UX; enforcement is server-side. A guard can stop a user from seeing a screen; only the server can stop them from *doing the thing*. Interviewers who probe this distinction are looking for whether you understand that the ID in the URL is attacker-controlled input.
keyConcepts: Three layers, and what each one can do
The next parameter â€” the vulnerability everyone forgets
The client router must also not render the protected component
Token storage, briefly (full treatment in PHASE 7 and 4.6.9)
Production and operational

Centralise: one requireUser/requirePermission per route module, and a lint/review rule that a route with data access must have a loader that calls it. Route-level guards are the most commonly forgotten security control in SPAs because there is no compile error when you skip one.
Cache-Control: private, no-store and Vary: Cookie on authenticated responses; a CDN-cached authenticated page is a data breach (4.6.5 scenario 9).
Guard the *server actions* and *API handlers* too â€” a route guard protects the UI, not the endpoint. This is Broken Access Control / IDOR territory in OWASP (PHASE 7).
Session expiry mid-session: an API layer that detects a 401 broadcasts to all tabs (BroadcastChannel) and triggers one redirect, rather than N tabs each redirecting.
Log denials with user + resource + permission: 403 spikes are the signal for a privilege-escalation attempt or a broken role mapping.

Test: for every protected route, an integration test that asserts (a) unauthenticated â†’ redirect, (b) authenticated but unauthorised â†’ 403, (c) authorised â†’ data, and (d) *authenticated as user A requesting user B's resource â†’ 403* â€” that last one is the test most teams do not write and it is the one that catches real breaches.
"You hid the admin button. Is the app secure?" (No â€” explain the three layers and where enforcement lives.)
commonMistakes: Guarding only in components; a role check where an object check was needed; validating next insufficiently; caching authenticated HTML; not guarding the server action/API; redirect loops from a loader that fetches without cookies.
component-only guards; broad middleware matchers; no object-level checks; unvalidated next; authenticated HTML in a shared cache.

tradeoffs: Edge guards are fast and prevent disclosure but are limited by what they can read (cookies/headers, no DB), and a broad matcher adds latency to every request. Router guards are precise and can make authorisation decisions with full context, but only after the app is loaded. Component guards are pure UX. The correct architecture uses all three with one rule: the server check is the only one that matters; the other two reduce wasted requests and avoid embarrassing flashes.

topics.title: Lazy loading routes and code splitting at the route boundary
topics.description: Route-level code splitting is the discipline of making each route's *component module* a separate bundle, downloaded when that route is first needed. It is the single highest-leverage performance technique in a routed SPA, because routes are the natural boundaries of both code and data.

tradeoffs: Route splitting reduces initial bytes and improves time-to-interactive, at the cost of: one more round trip on first navigation to each route (mitigated by prefetch), the ChunkLoadError class of bugs, and complexity around shared chunks (a bug-fix to a shared dependency invalidates every chunk that uses it, so you want long-lived vendor chunks and immutable hashed filenames). The failure mode of over-splitting is worse than under-splitting on a fast connection and better on a slow one â€” so measure on the slowest network your users actually have (4.6.8 RUM, not lab).

topics.description: Navigation hooks are the router's imperative API for programmatic navigation (navigate), the current location (useLocation), params (useParams), and navigation state (useNavigation, useNavigationType). Scroll restoration is the policy of putting the user back where they were when they hit Back â€” including the hard cases where the content was virtualised or lazily loaded and the saved offset no longer means anything.

tradeoffs: Restoring by key is simple and works for stable lists; it needs history.state or a ref map and it does not survive a reload (sessionStorage does). Anchored restoration is correct and works with mutations and virtualisation; it costs a fetch of the containing page and a measure-after-render step. Programmatic navigation with state is convenient but the state is lost on reload and cannot hold large data (structured-clone limits, and it ends up in the history entry visible to the user). Relative navigation (..) is refactor-safe but confusing when read literally â€” prefer it inside nested layouts.

topics.title: Parallel routes, intercepting routes, and modal routing
topics.description: Parallel routes render multiple independent route slots into the *same layout at the same time* â€” so one layout can host, say, a feed and an authenticated sidebar that load and refresh independently. Intercepting routes render one slot *in place of* its normal position when the navigation came from a specific origin (a <Link> from the feed, a form submission) while falling back to the normal position on a hard navigation (a direct URL load, a refresh, a paste). Together they give you the "modal routing" pattern that makes a photo lightbox feel instant while keeping the URL shareable and the deep link correct.

Slot content duplicated across slots (double fetch). Intercepting a route that should have been a real page.

tradeoffs: Parallel routes buy independent loading/error boundaries and independent refresh semantics inside one layout â€” genuinely useful for dashboards (a slow "usage" widget must not block the feed) and for authenticated chrome. They cost: the slot props are unusual and easy to get wrong, the fallback requirement is easy to miss, and debuggers show duplicated fetches when a slot renders on a navigation it should not have. Intercepting routes buy the best modal UX in web apps; they cost the most complex routing mental model in any framework, two code paths per modal (soft and hard), and the requirement that every modal be a *real route* with its own data loading â€” which is more work than a component, and exactly why it is worth it (the alternative is a modal that cannot be shared or server-rendered).

topics.title: Deep linking, URL design, and query-param state
topics.description: Deep linking is the ability to open any state of the app by URL alone, on a cold load, in a new tab, shared with someone else, months later. URL design is deciding which state belongs in the path, which in the query string, which in neither, and how to make all of it canonical.
keyConcepts: The URL contract â€” the design decisions, in order

Identity in the path, view state in the query. The path says *what exists*; the query says *how you are looking at it*. A URL in the query should never be the only way to identify a resource (an id in the query can be shared incorrectly and is invisible to crawlers).

The URL must decide what the server returns. ?page=3 must fetch page 3 server-side, or a shared link shows page 1 (the classic "deep link loads the wrong page" bug). Similarly for filters and sorting on any indexable page.

Canonicalise. Omit defaults (?page=1 â†’ /tasks), normalise parameter order, one canonical spelling of a filter (status=open not statuses=open&open=true), and redirect non-canonical URLs with a 301/308 so link equity and analytics do not split. Never have two URLs render identical content.
One spelling per thing, forever. Renaming a path segment means a redirect map (old â†’ new, permanent) â€” do it once, keep it forever.

URLs are a public API. They appear in emails, support tickets, QR codes, printed receipts, and Slack messages. They must be readable, stable, and free of secrets (4.6.9). Human-readable slugs for public content (/blog/optimistic-updates-rollback) with a numeric id hidden behind them.

Pagination state is URL state, and its format is a product decision: page numbers for admin tables (?page=3), cursor for feeds (?after=â€¦ â€” visible but ugly; some products keep the cursor out of the URL and accept losing back-navigation within a feed). Be explicit about which you chose and why.

Tabs and wizards: ?tab=history is deep-linkable (good for support and for emails linking to "the invoices tab"); a wizard step is usually URL state too (/checkout/2/payment) so Back works and a reload does not lose progress â€” but that means you must validate which steps the user may reach (4.3.7/4.5.5).
Sort direction: use an explicit prefix (sort=-due) rather than a separate param (dir=desc) so a sort is one atomic value; or use sort=due&dir=asc if you need both â€” pick one and be consistent.
Deep-link correctness checklist
Interaction with the query cache
Production and operational
commonMistakes: Filters in a store instead of the URL. Defaults left in the URL. Two URLs for the same view. A deep link that fetches page 1 regardless of ?page=. Search text pushed on every keystroke. ?q= in a path with unescaped special characters. Analytics counting a filter change as a pageview.
store-based filters; no canonical form; page=1 shipped in links; unvalidated params reaching the API.

tradeoffs: Rich URLs cost verbosity (a 90-character query string), require validation and canonicalisation, and force you to think about which state is durable â€” but they buy shareability, Back-button correctness, SSR/crawlability, analytics attribution, reduced server state (nothing to persist per user), and supportability ("open this URL and you'll see what I see"). Thin URLs (everything in memory) are faster to build and look cleaner in code, and break everything above. The middle ground most products choose: *path for identity, query for view state, ephemeral UI state (open panels, hover, focused field) nowhere.* One more consideration: search-relevant state in the query string is indexable, so if a filter is not meant to be indexed, put it in the query but noindex that combination â€” and be aware that in practice this generates crawl waste.

topics.title: Router comparison: React Router, TanStack Router, Next.js App Router, Remix
topics.description: A router comparison is a set of decisions about *where the route table lives*, *who owns data loading*, *how caching works*, *how much framework is imposed*, and *what you must know about rendering*. These four options are not interchangeable: two are routers you mount in your own app, two are frameworks that own the whole application.
keyConcepts: The comparison
How to choose, in the order a staff engineer actually uses it

Do you need server rendering, SEO, or a CDN-cached public site? If yes â†’ a framework (Next.js App Router, Remix). If no â†’ a library (React Router, TanStack Router) and you keep your own deploy story. *This single question eliminates half the options.*

Are you already on Next.js? Stay on Next.js unless you have a named, measurable blocker. Migration cost is the dominant term, and Next's weaknesses (implicit caching) are now well-documented and cacheable.

Do you want compile-time route/param/search typing across a large app? â†’ TanStack Router. It is the strongest typing story in React routing, and defaultPreload: 'intent' gives you prefetching for free.

Do you want maximum control and the smallest surface, and are you already rendering your own HTML or using a non-standard renderer? â†’ React Router. It is a router, not a framework, and it composes with anything.
Do you want explicit data flow, progressive enhancement, and no magic caching? â†’ Remix / RR7 framework mode. Every request's data flow is visible in one file.
Do you need parallel/intercepting routes (modal-over-feed at scale)? â†’ Next.js App Router (or build it yourself, which is real work).

"What does Next's implicit caching cost you, and how do you mitigate it?"
"What is the strongest argument for TanStack Router?"
"What does 'progressive enhancement' mean here, and which router gives it to you for free?"
commonMistakes: choosing by popularity; ignoring who owns the cache; treating a router as if it also solved data fetching; migrating for a framework preference rather than a named defect.

tradeoffs: Next.js: implicit, rule-based caching that has changed defaults across versions and is the single largest source of "why is my data stale" incidents; a client/server boundary you must reason about constantly ('use client' at the top of a file is a big hammer); a large runtime; and a fast-moving release cadence. Mitigation: keep data access in server components, make cache policy explicit and documented per route, and pin versions.

React Router: you own the cache, the SSR strategy, the error handling, and the file conventions â€” which is freedom and also work. Mitigation: adopt a data layer with opinions (TanStack Query), a route-error-boundary convention, and a lazy-route policy (4.5.6).
TanStack Router: the plugin/codegen is a new moving part, and the type inference is a build-time cost; in exchange you get params/search typed end to end and excellent preload/intent behaviour.
Remix: its loader/action model is its greatest strength and its main constraint â€” you must learn to think per-request, and nested-route data dependencies take a moment to internalise.

topics.title: File-based routing and route organisation
topics.description: File-based routing derives the route table from the directory tree â€” the filesystem *is* the router configuration. Add a file, get a route; delete a file, the route is gone; move a file, the URL changes. Nothing declares a path, a layout chain, or a param list in JS, because there is no second place where the URL can be written down and drift out of sync. The important part is that a convention is only as good as its escape hatches: route groups, layout files, dynamic segments, optional catch-alls, and a documented way to opt out (routes.ts).
keyConcepts: Production and operational
"What do route groups do, and when do you need one?"
"How do you keep a route rename from breaking production?"
"What does codegen buy you that a JS route array cannot?"
"Where do you draw the line between convention and configuration?"
"How would you audit which routes exist and which are protected?"
Shared setup for most drills
Drill 1 â€” Two components, same key, mount simultaneously
Drill 2 â€” staleTime: 0, navigate away and back in 2 seconds
Drill 3 â€” Same, but staleTime: 60_000
Drill 4 â€” gcTime: 0 with an unmounted entry
Drill 8 â€” Two optimistic mutations on the same list, second fails
commonMistakes: Two files resolving to the same URL without a group; assuming a group creates a path segment (it does not); putting request state in a layout and wondering why it survives navigation; using (group) for auth instead of a real check; renaming a folder without redirects; mixing generated and hand-written routes without a documented single writer; and relying on the folder name for security.
treating the convention as enforcement; no redirect discipline on moves; two writers for the route tree; ignoring that optional catch-all can swallow its siblings' URLs.

tradeoffs: File-based routing buys: no config file to merge-conflict, an enumerable route set, automatic per-route code splitting, and â€” when codegen is involved â€” compile-time checking of paths, params, and search. It costs: a build step you did not write, a learning curve for the conventions (group vs folder, [id] vs :id vs $id), the fact that moving a file changes a URL (so "just reorganise" becomes a production incident without redirects), limited expressiveness for anything irregular (deeply conditional matching, versioned APIs with a custom ranking function â€” which is exactly why TanStack Router lets you drop to a code-defined route, and why Next lets you write a route.ts handler outside the tree). The rule of thumb I give teams: convention for the 90%, an explicit escape hatch for the 10%, and never both for the same route.

topics.title: Design systems
topics.description: A design system is a versioned, cross-product collection of decisions â€” tokens, primitives, components, patterns, documentation â€” plus the governance that keeps those decisions consistent. Canonical entry for design principles and visual language: PHASE 1 â†’ Communication; here we talk engineering.
keyConcepts: What a design system is
A single source of truth for visual and interaction decisions, encoded as code where possible (tokens, components, lints).
A contract with a versioning policy: consumers declare which major version they are on and get a migration path.
A product of an organisation: it exists because five teams were solving the same modal focus-trap bug five different ways.
An accessibility enforcement point: primitives are where keyboard and screen-reader behaviour is proved once.
What a design system is NOT
Not a Figma file with a colour palette. Designers' files are an input, not the deliverable â€” code is where behaviour lives.
Not a "component library with nice buttons". It includes *patterns* (how components combine to accomplish a task), *content guidelines* (empty states, error copy), and *governance*.
Not a monolith of 200 exported components. A system that nobody can navigate is a system nobody adopts.
Not a marketing term for "we use Tailwind". Tailwind is a styling mechanism; a design system is the decisions plus the contract.
The anatomy: token â†’ primitive â†’ component â†’ pattern â†’ page
Design tokens
commonMistakes: calling Figma the design system; letting product code reference primitives; assuming dark: class variants scale past a handful of components; adding props instead of slots; deprecating without a codemod or a migration deadline; treating accessibility as a checklist at the end; versioning by "how big the diff looks" instead of by API compatibility; measuring adoption by "did we write it" instead of "is it used".
practiceTasks: build a token pipeline: author 40 tokens in JSON, emit CSS custom properties + a TS object + a markdown table; define a light and a dark theme; write the tier-boundary lint; then implement Button, Input, and Dialog consuming only semantic tokens, with axe passing and a --brand switch at runtime with no rebuild. Measure the CSS output size for one theme and justify whether you shipped both or generated one at build time.

- **Customisation cost drops to near zero**, because customisation is a diff you control.

    field: c.key, headerName: c.header, flex: c.flex ?? 1, sortable: c.sortable !== false,
    renderCell: c.render ? (p) => c.render!(p.row as Row) : undefined,
  }));
  return <Grid rows={rows} columns={cols} onSortModelChange={onSortChange as never} {...rest} />;

topics.title: Storybook
topics.description: A workshop for UI components in isolation â€” a static site per component, where every variant, state, and edge case is a *story* that can be rendered, reviewed, tested, and diffed.
keyConcepts: Stories vs stories of stories
A story is one named, parameterised state of a component (Primary, WithError, Loading, LongLabel, RTL, ZeroItems).

A story of stories is the *coverage requirement*: the argument that a component's stories must enumerate its state space, not just its happy path. A mature component library has a story per state (default, hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, error, empty, over-long content, RTL, high-contrast, reduced-motion) â€” that is the real contract.

Docs pages group stories and add prose; autodocs generate the API table (props, types, defaults, descriptions) from the component's TypeScript types plus JSDoc. Autodocs means your docs table rots less than a hand-written props table â€” the machine-reads-types part is the win; the descriptions still need a human.
MDX mixes prose with live stories, which is how you document "when to use / when not to use" with an example rather than a screenshot.
Interaction testing with play
The a11y addon, and what it cannot catch
Keyboard operability of a custom widget (does Tab order make sense? does Escape close?).
Focus visibility and focus-trap correctness in dynamic content.
Screen-reader announcement quality and reading order (e.g. a live region that exists but announces nothing useful).
Whether the accessible name is *meaningful* ("Click here").
Timing and motion problems, or zoom/reflow at 400%.
commonMistakes: treating Storybook as documentation only, or as documentation that lives in a wiki; writing one story per component instead of one per state; live API calls in stories; flaky visual baselines papered over with tolerance thresholds; assuming axe means accessible; a Storybook per app in a monorepo.
practiceTasks: write Dialog and Select with full state stories, add a play test per state that asserts focus behaviour, add axe, then run everything in CI on a deliberately broken version (remove the focus trap, remove the label) and confirm the pipeline catches each defect. Finally, set up visual regression, deliberately introduce a flaky story, and write down what caused the flake and how you fixed it.

interviewQuestions.text: What problem does Storybook solve that unit tests do not?
What is a "story of stories" and why does it matter?
How do args and argTypes differ, and what does autodocs take from your types?
Why does a `play` function test something a jsdom unit test cannot?
What fraction of accessibility problems does the axe addon catch, and what does it miss?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: axe-core automates a well-defined subset of accessibility rules, and it is excellent at that subset. Decision: run it on every story in CI as a blocking gate for critical and serious violations, and pair it with a mandatory manual keyboard and screen-reader pass per component release. Reasoning: the addon catches mechanical failures â€” missing accessible names, invalid ARIA, missing labels, some contrast â€” which are numerous and entirely mechanical, so automation gives immediate value at near-zero marginal cost. What it cannot judge is interaction: whether a custom listbox's arrow-key behaviour matches the ARIA pattern, whether focus moves into a dialog and returns to the invoker on close, whether the focus ring is visible against the actual background, whether a live region announces a change meaningfully, or whether the accessible name is any good at all. Failure scenario: we ship a combobox that passes axe with a correct role and aria-expanded but does nothing on ArrowDown, so a keyboard or screen-reader user cannot reach any option â€” green pipeline, unusable product. Trade-offs: full manual testing per component is expensive and inconsistent, which is why I want one documented manual checklist per component archetype (dialog, combobox, tabs, table) and a shared vocabulary, rather than 'test accessibility' as a slogan. Alternative: shift automated effort to keyboard-interaction assertions inside play, which mechanises part of the manual check by simulating a real user with userEvent."

interviewQuestions.text: How do you make visual regression baselines stable? Give four concrete causes of flake and their fixes.
Should visual regression block a merge?
How do you run one Storybook for a monorepo?
How do you document a *published* component package so docs cannot drift from versions?
Storybook build time is 8 minutes. What do you measure first?
How do you stop stories rotting when nobody is motivated?
When would you deliberately *not* use Storybook?

|---|---|

topics.title: Micro-frontends
topics.description: An architectural pattern where a single-page application is decomposed into independently built, deployed, and owned sub-applications that are composed at runtime into one user-facing product. Canonical backend-side treatment: PHASE 11 â†’ Architectural Styles â†’ Microfrontends; here the *frontend mechanics and costs*.
keyConcepts: Real motivations
Independent deploy cadence. Multiple teams must ship on their own schedules through one shared release train without coordinating merges. This is the strongest legitimate driver.

Organisational autonomy at scale. Team boundaries *caused by* code ownership need: "if you can't deploy it alone, you can't be on call for it alone." At ~50+ engineers across overlapping surfaces, deployment coupling is the real cost of a shared frontend repo.
Legacy incremental migration. A 400k-line Angular app gets a new React surface without a rewrite. Strangler-fig the frontend (PHASE 11).

Domain boundaries that genuinely differ. Billing is a checkout with a totally different UX and lifecycle from an analytics dashboard; merging them into one bundle and one deploy is a merge of risk profiles, not just code.

Technology heterogeneity as a *by-product*, never as a goal. "We use React in the new thing because the new thing is React" is fine; "we split so each team picks its own framework" is a cost with no user benefit and enormous tax.
Real costs

Runtime inconsistency: the shell and remotes were built at different times against different dependency versions. Two copies of React â†’ hooks errors; two copies of a token system â†’ visual mismatch; two router versions â†’ navigation bugs.
Dependency duplication and bundle bloat. If each MFE is independently built and each bundles its own framework, you ship 3Ã— React. Sizing becomes a first-class concern (see sharing/singletons).

CSS isolation is genuinely hard. Options are: CSS Modules or scoped styles per MFE (works, but you lose cross-MFE overrides like theming and typography), Shadow DOM (real isolation, but breaks global design-token inheritance, form controls, fonts, and is awkward for SSR), BEM naming discipline, or a strict "no global CSS outside the shell" rule. Every real implementation picks one and suffers its trade-off.

Cross-team coordination cost. Contract changes, shared component releases, and release-order dependencies reappear as distributed-systems problems: you need versioning, compatibility windows, and deprecation.
Testing. End-to-end tests must test the *composition*, which is now nondeterministic and version-skewed. Unit/component tests stay inside the MFE; integration tests need both sides deployed.
commonMistakes: adopting micro-frontends for "scalability" or "team autonomy" without a release-cadence problem; leaving routing unowned; ignoring the React singleton; assuming client-side composition is SEO-safe; migrating the shell before one remote works end to end; not budgeting the runtime dependency.
practiceTasks: build a shell with two routes, each loading a separately built "remote" (two Vite builds with a tiny federated-style loader), sharing a singleton React, a shared token stylesheet, and a typed postMessage event bus. Then break it on purpose: ship remote v2 with a changed shared-component prop and no shell release, and document the failure and the compatibility fix. Add a trace-id breadcrumb in both apps and show the correlated Sentry issue.

interviewQuestions.text: What problems do micro-frontends genuinely solve? Which one is strongest?
List the costs. Which do teams underestimate?
Build-time vs runtime composition: when each?
How does the shell own routing, and what breaks if two MFEs disagree about routes?
How do you share React across MFEs, and what fails if you get it wrong?
How do you isolate CSS between remotes? What does Shadow DOM break?
Design cross-MFE communication. When is URL state enough?
Auth across three apps on the same parent domain: your approach?
Your shell v2 ships while remote v1 is still deployed. What are the failure modes and mitigations?
What is a compatibility contract between a shell and a remote?
How do you trace one user action across four codebases?
Migrate a monolith: order the steps and pick the first slice.

- **Shell owns the router.** The shell holds all routes; MFEs receive navigation intent as props or via a shared router instance. Best DX and best focus/announcement behaviour. - **MFE owns a route prefix.** The shell lazy-loads the remote on first navigation. Cheaper shell, but the shell must know which prefixes map to which remote (a route manifest again) and you must handle deep links, unknown routes, and the "shell loaded, remote 404s" state.
- **Hybrid (most common):** shell owns top-level navigation and auth; each MFE owns sub-routes and its own internal router instance, with navigation events bubbled to the shell for breadcrumbs/analytics.

**Sharing dependencies and singletons.** With runtime composition you have to decide, per shared dependency:
- **Singleton (must be one instance):** React (hooks break with two copies), the router, the i18n runtime, the design-token provider, the analytics client, the auth/session client, the query cache. Two routers means two histories.
- **Shareable (duplication is acceptable):** date libraries, validation schemas, pure utilities.
- Module Federation's `shared` config with an eager/required singleton version and a fallback is the mechanism; `requiredVersion` with `singleton: true` and a version range is the practical setting, and you must understand the failure mode: a version mismatch either loads the shell's copy (potentially breaking an MFE expecting a newer API) or throws at load. 1. **URL and route state.** The cheapest and most robust channel. Encode what the other app needs in the query string or path; nothing to wire, naturally shareable/bookmarkable, survives reloads. Prefer this whenever it works.
2. **Custom DOM events on `document`.** Loose coupling, no shared imports, but untyped, globally visible, and unaudited. Wrap in a typed `emit`/`on` helper with a naming convention and payload schemas, and make listeners idempotent.
3. **A shared state library** (a tiny store or a pub/sub package) when several apps need a broadcast channel (e.g. "cart changed", "session expiring"). 4. **A shared service package** (auth client, API client) â€” normal dependency, just versioned.
5. **What to avoid:** MFE A importing MFE B's internals. It converts two deployables into one, and the whole independence story dies.
Also handle the **multi-instance case**: three instances of the same MFE on one page means event names and DOM ids must be namespaced per instance. This bites with repeated widgets, and it is a great interview trap.

**Auth across apps.** Options:
- **Shared cookie session** (canonical: PHASE 7 â†’ Auth Mechanisms): one `HttpOnly` `Secure` `SameSite=Lax` session cookie on the parent domain; every MFE calls the same auth service and gets the same identity. Best answer for same-origin composition. Requires CSRF protection on state-changing requests (cross-ref PHASE 7).
- **Shared SDK in the shell** that owns login/logout and broadcasts expiry so MFEs don't each implement a refresh loop.
- **Bearer tokens per app** (each MFE has its own client credentials) â€” isolates blast radius but multiplies token lifetimes and revocation problems; only if the MFEs are genuinely separate products (possibly cross-origin, then it's SSO/OIDC and cross-ref PHASE 7).

2. **Introduce the shell as a thin router + auth + layout**, serving the existing monolith for unmigrated routes (an iframe, or a reverse proxy path that serves the old app).
3. **Extract a route at a time**, highest-churn first (that is where the coupling hurts), and prefer a route with low shared-state interaction (a settings page, a reports view) over the checkout.

- No platform/infra capacity to own the runtime, the shell, and the CI.
- Heavy real-time coupling (multiplayer editing, trading) where a single coherent state model matters more than deploy independence.
The honest interview framing: micro-frontends convert **code-level coupling into operational and runtime coupling**. 2. List the costs. Which do teams underestimate?
3. Build-time vs runtime composition: when each?
4. How does the shell own routing, and what breaks if two MFEs disagree about routes?
5. How do you share React across MFEs, and what fails if you get it wrong?
6. How do you isolate CSS between remotes? What does Shadow DOM break?
7. Design cross-MFE communication. When is URL state enough?
8. Auth across three apps on the same parent domain: your approach?
9. Your shell v2 ships while remote v1 is still deployed. What are the failure modes and mitigations?
10. What is a compatibility contract between a shell and a remote?
11. How do you trace one user action across four codebases?
12. Migrate a monolith: order the steps and pick the first slice.
13. Your team has 12 engineers and wants micro-frontends. What do you say?
14. When is a modular monolith the better answer, and how do you enforce its boundaries?
15. What does an MFE outage look like, and how should the shell behave?
16. How do micro-frontends affect SEO and first load, and what do you do about it?

**Model answer, Q13:** "Context: a 12-engineer team with one product, two deploys a week, and a bundle that is not actually the bottleneck. At 12 engineers the coordination overhead of a shell, a runtime loader, N pipelines, compatibility contracts, cross-repo version skew, and composition-level E2E tests exceeds the release-coupling problem it solves. The hidden costs are real: duplicate React copies, CSS isolation compromises, fragmented observability, and a class of version-skew bugs that are miserable to debug. Then break it on purpose: ship remote v2 with a changed shared-component prop and no shell release, and document the failure and the compatibility fix. Add a trace-id breadcrumb in both apps and show the correlated Sentry issue.

topics.title: Frontend project structure and boundaries
topics.description: Frontend project structure and boundaries within Design systems.
keyConcepts: Feature-based vs type-based folders
Layering and dependency direction
Dependencies point downward only. shared/lib never imports from features; a feature never imports from another feature's internals.
features are private by default. Another feature wanting your code goes through your feature's public index.ts, or you promote the shared piece to shared/.

app is composition only: providers, routing, error boundaries, layout. It should contain no business logic â€” if app/ has if (user.role === 'admin'), that belongs in a feature or a permission module.
shared/lib is framework-free if you want to test it without a renderer and reuse it in workers.
Enforcing boundaries mechanically
Circular dependency detection
Module boundaries vs folder names
Barrels (index.ts) and why they hurt

Tree-shaking degrades. With sideEffects metadata and proper ESM, unused exports *can* be shaken, but barrel files create large re-export graphs that some bundlers resolve poorly, and any barrel member with a side effect (a polyfill, a window guard) is retained, dragging its whole subtree in. The reliable statement for an interview: barrels make it harder for bundlers to prove a module is unused, and the cost grows with barrel size and import-path depth.
Build/watch cost. In a monorepo or a large app, a barrel re-export of many files turns any change into a large invalidation graph (dev-server restarts, slow type-check, watch-mode thrash).
commonMistakes: mixing type-based and feature-based conventions without a rule; adding barrels "for cleanliness"; relying on review instead of lint for boundaries; promoting a single-consumer helper to a shared package; a big-bang restructure on a live codebase; tests in a mirrored __tests__ tree that drift.
practiceTasks: take an existing app (or scaffold one with 3 features), add feature-based folders, eslint-plugin-boundaries rules, a madge --circular CI step, and alias config across tsconfig/Vitest/ESLint. Then, one file at a time, move code into the new structure with the suite green at every commit, and record the wall-clock time the lint rule saved you versus the time the rules cost on new code.

interviewQuestions.text: Feature-based vs type-based folders: what does each optimise for and break on?
Draw your layering and say which direction imports are allowed.
How do you enforce boundaries without relying on code review?
What creates circular dependencies, and how do you detect them in CI?
Why do barrels hurt tree-shaking and build times? What's the compromise?
interviewQuestions.answer: "Context: barrels are the reflex fix for 'too many import paths' and they are a real build-performance footgun. Decision: barrels at package and feature boundaries only, never in leaf directories. Reasoning: a barrel creates a re-export graph that the bundler must analyse to decide what is unused; the bigger the barrel, the more of it must be proven side-effect-free before anything can be dropped, and any module in the graph with a side effect (a polyfill, a global registration) is retained along with its imports. On top of that, in watch mode and in monorepo builds, a single changed file invalidates every module that re-exports it, so a barrel at the top of shared/lib turns one edit into a large rebuild. 8. What is a package's public API, and how do you keep it small?
9. How should feature flags be structured in code, and what breaks if they aren't?
10. How do tests mirror folder structure, and what does awkward testing tell you?
11. You have 400 files in `utils/`. Describe the incremental fix over two weeks.
12. When is a big-bang restructure justified?
13. How do you use `CODEOWNERS` to protect a design system from feature teams?
14. What does a deep import past a public entry cost you, and how do you block it?

**Model answer, Q5:** "Context: barrels are the reflex fix for 'too many import paths' and they are a real build-performance footgun. Decision: barrels at package and feature boundaries only, never in leaf directories. Reasoning: a barrel creates a re-export graph that the bundler must analyse to decide what is unused; the bigger the barrel, the more of it must be proven side-effect-free before anything can be dropped, and any module in the graph with a side effect (a polyfill, a global registration) is retained along with its imports. On top of that, in watch mode and in monorepo builds, a single changed file invalidates every module that re-exports it, so a barrel at the top of `shared/lib` turns one edit into a large rebuild. Cycle detection also gets harder because the cycle runs through the barrel entry. Trade-offs: this costs a bit of import ergonomics â€” consumers write `import { formatDate } from '@/shared/lib/dates'` rather than `'@/shared/lib'` â€” and it means discipline, since one lazy barrel will be added eventually and the rule must be enforced. Failure scenario: a team adds a root barrel for convenience; `shared/lib` ends up importing a module that touches `window` for a Node/worker path, so the whole graph lands in the initial chunk for every route, and the app's LCP regresses by 180 kB with no visible cause. Alternative: keep the ergonomic barrel but split per-package with `exports` maps and `sideEffects: false`, and verify with the bundler's stats that the initial chunk actually dropped â€” measure, don't believe."

**Mistakes:** mixing type-based and feature-based conventions without a rule; adding barrels "for cleanliness"; relying on review instead of lint for boundaries; promoting a single-consumer helper to a shared package; a big-bang restructure on a live codebase; tests in a mirrored `__tests__` tree that drift.

**Mini task:** take an existing app (or scaffold one with 3 features), add feature-based folders, `eslint-plugin-boundaries` rules, a `madge --circular` CI step, and alias config across tsconfig/Vitest/ESLint. Then, one file at a time, move code into the new structure with the suite green at every commit, and record the wall-clock time the lint rule saved you versus the time the rules cost on new code.
